We have \begin{align*} B & = \left\{ x + \iota y \in \mathbb{C} : \text{ Re} \left( (x + \iota y)^2 \right) = 2 \right\} \\ & = \left\{ x + \iota y \in \mathbb{C} : \text{ Re} \left( x^2 - y^2 + 2\iota xy \right) = 2 \right\} \\ & = \left\{ x + \iota y \in \mathbb{C} : x^2 - y^2 = 2 \right\}. \end{align*} The above set is a hyperbola in the complex plane.
  3. The given set is $C = \left\{ z \in \mathbb{C} : \text{ Im} \left( \frac{1}{z} \right) = \frac{1}{4} \right\} $. We have \begin{align*} C & = \left\{ x + \iota y \in \mathbb{C} : \text{ Im} \left( \frac{1}{x + \iota y} \right) = \frac{1}{4} \right\} \\ & = \left\{ x + \iota y \in \mathbb{C} : \text{ Im} \left( \frac{x - \iota y}{x^2 + y^2} \right) = \frac{1}{4} \right\} \\ & = \left\{ x + \iota y \in \mathbb{C} : \frac{-y}{x^2 + y^2} = \frac{1}{4} \right\} \\ & = \left\{ x + \iota y \in \mathbb{C} : -4y = x^2 + y^2 \text{ and } x^2 + y^2 \neq 0\right\} \\ & = \left\{ x + \iota y \in \mathbb{C} : x^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 4 \right\} \setminus \{ 0 \} . \end{align*} The above set is a circle with center at $(0, -2)$ and radius $2$.
  4. The set $D = \left\{ z \in \mathbb{C} : \vert z \vert = \text{ Re } z + 1 \right\} $ is given by \begin{align*} D & = \left\{ x + \iota y \in \mathbb{C} : \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = x + 1 \right\} \\ & = \left\{ x + \iota y \in \mathbb{C} : x^2 + y^2 = x^2 + 2x + 1 \right\} \\ & = \left\{ x + \iota y \in \mathbb{C} : y^2 = 2x + 1 \right\} \\ & = \left\{ x + \iota y \in \mathbb{C} : x = \frac{y^2 - 1}{2} \right\}. \end{align*} The above set is a parabola in the complex plane.
  5. The set $E = \left\{ z \in \mathbb{C} : \vert z - 2 \vert = \vert 1 - 2 \bar{z} \vert \right\} $ is given by \begin{align*} E & = \left\{ x + \iota y \in \mathbb{C} : \sqrt{(x - 2)^2 + y^2} = \sqrt{(1 - 2x)^2 + 4y^2} \right\} \\ & = \left\{ x + \iota y \in \mathbb{C} : (x - 2)^2 + y^2 = (1 - 2x)^2 + 4y^2 \right\} \\ & = \left\{ x + \iota y \in \mathbb{C} : x^2 - 4x + 4 + y^2 = 1 - 4x + 4x^2 + 4y^2 \right\} \\ & = \left\{ x + \iota y \in \mathbb{C} : 3x^2 + 3y^2 = 3 \right\} \\ & = \left\{ x + \iota y \in \mathbb{C} : x^2 + y^2 = 1 \right\}. \end{align*} The above set is a circle with center at $(0, 0)$ and radius $1$.

problems.title: Contour Integration using Residue Theorem
problems.problem:
Evaluate the contour integral
\[
    \oint_C \frac{e^z}{z^2 + 1} \, dz,
\]
where \( C \) is the positively oriented unit circle \( |z| = 1 \).
problems.solution:
The function \( f(z) = \frac{e^z}{z^2 + 1} \) has singularities where \( z^2 + 1 = 0 \), i.e., at \( z = \pm \iota \). Among these, only \( z = \iota \) lies inside the unit circle \( |z| = 1 \). Thus, the integral can be evaluated using the residue theorem which say that the integral of a function \( f(z) \) around a simple closed curve \( C \) is given by: \[ \oint_C f(z) \, \mathrm{d} z = 2\pi \iota \sum_{k=1}^{n} \text{Res}(f, z_k), \] where \( z_k \) are the poles of \( f(z) \) inside \( C \).
In this problem, since there is only one pole $z = \iota $ inside the curve $\vert z \vert = 1$, the integral will be \[ \oint_C \frac{e^z}{z^2 + 1} \, dz = 2\pi \iota \cdot \text{Res}(f, \iota ). \]
Let us find the residue at \( z = \iota \). Note that $z = \iota $ is a simple pole of the function. We recall that the residue of a function \( f(z) \) at a simple pole \( z = z_0 \) is given by: \[ \text{Res}(f, z_0) = \lim_{z \to z_0} (z - z_0) f(z). \] Therefore, \[ \text{Res}(f, \iota ) = \lim_{z \to \iota } (z - \iota ) \frac{e^z}{(z - \iota )(z + \iota )}. \] Simplifying, \[ \text{Res}(f, \iota ) = \lim_{z \to \iota } \frac{e^z}{z + \iota } = \frac{e^{\iota } }{2\iota }. \] By the residue theorem, \[ \oint_C \frac{e^z}{z^2 + 1} \, dz = 2\pi \iota \cdot \frac{e^{\iota } }{2\iota } = \pi e^{\iota } . \]

problems.title: Graphing Sets in the Complex Plane
problems.problem:
Find the real and imaginary part of the following functions $f: \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C} $.
  1. $f(z) = \sin z$
  2. $f(z) = z^2 \cos z$
  3. $f(z) = z^3 + 5z - 1$
  4. $f(z) = \frac{z^2 + 1}{z - 1}$
  5. $f(z) = \vert z \vert \bar{z}$
problems.solution:
A general method to find the real and imaginary part of the complex function is to write $z = x + \iota y$ and then express the function in terms of $x$ and $y$. Separate the real and imaginary parts.
  1. For \( f(z) = \sin z \): \begin{align*} f(z) & = \frac{e^{\iota z} - e^{-\iota z}}{2\iota } \\[1ex] & = \frac{e^{\iota x - y} - e^{-\iota x + y}}{2\iota } \\[1ex] & = \frac{e^{\iota x} e^{-y} - e^{-\iota x} e^{y}}{2\iota } \\[1ex] & = \frac{e^{-y} \left( \cos x + \iota \sin x \right) - e^y \left( \cos x - \iota \sin x \right) }{2 \iota }\\ & = \frac{e^y + e^{-y} }{2} \sin x + \iota \frac{e^y - e^{-y} }{2 } \cos x. \end{align*} Therefore,
    \begin{align*} \text{Re} (f(z)) & = \frac{e^y + e^{-y} }{2} \sin x = \cosh y \sin x, \\[1ex] \text{Im} (f(z)) & = \frac{e^y - e^{-y} }{2 } \cos x = \sinh y \cos x. \end{align*}
  2. For the function \( f(z) = z^2 \cos z \): \[ z^2 = (x + \iota y)^2 = x^2 - y^2 + 2\iota xy, \] and by the same method or using the trigonometric identities we have \begin{align*} \cos z & = \cos (x + \iota y) \\ & = \cos x \cos \iota y - \sin x \sin \iota y. \end{align*} Since $x$ and $y$ are real, we have \begin{align*} & \cos(iy)=\frac{\exp(i^2y)+\exp(-i^2y)}{2}=\frac{\exp y+\exp(-y)}{2}=\cosh y \\ & \sin(iy)=\frac{\exp(i^2y)-\exp(-i^2y)}{2i}=-\frac{\exp y-\exp(-y)}{2i}=i\sinh y. \end{align*} Thus, \[ \cos z = \cos x \cosh y - \iota \sin x \sinh y. \] Therefore, \[ f(z) = (x^2 - y^2 + 2\iota xy)(\cos x \cosh y - \iota \sin x \sinh y). \] Separating the real and imaginary parts, we get:
    \begin{align*} \text{Re}(f(z)) & = (x^2 - y^2) \cos x \cosh y + 2xy \sin x \sinh y,\\ \text{Im}(f(z)) & = 2xy \cos x \sinh y - (x^2 - y^2) \sin x \cosh y. \end{align*}
  3. For \( f(z) = z^3 + 5z - 1 \): \begin{align*} z^3 & = (x + \iota y)^3 \\ & = x^3 + 3x^2 \iota y + 3x(\iota y)^2 + (\iota y)^3 \\ & = x^3 - 3xy^2 + \iota (3x^2 y - y^3). \end{align*} Therefore, \begin{align*} f(z) & = x^3 - 3xy^2 + \iota (3x^2 y - y^3) + 5 x + \iota 5y - 1 \\ & = x^3 - 3xy^2 + 5x - 1 + \iota (3x^2 y - y^3 + 5y). \end{align*} Thus,
    \begin{align*} \text{Re} (f(z)) & = x^3 - 3xy^2 + 5x - 1, \\ \text{Im} (f(z)) & = 3x^2 y - y^3 + 5y. \end{align*}
  4. For \( f(z) = \frac{z^2 + 1}{z - 1} \): \begin{align*} \frac{z^2 + 1}{z - 1} & = \frac{(x + \iota y)^2 + 1}{x + \iota y - 1} \\ & = \frac{(x^2 - y^2 + 1) + 2\iota xy}{(x - 1) + \iota y}. \end{align*} Multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, we get: \begin{align*} f(z) & = \frac{((x^2 - y^2 + 1) + 2\iota xy)((x - 1) - \iota y)}{(x - 1)^2 + y^2}. \end{align*} Separating the real and imaginary parts, we get:
    \begin{align*} \text{Re}(f(z)) & = \frac{(x^2 - y^2 + 1)(x - 1) + 2xy^2}{(x - 1)^2 + y^2} \\ \text{Im}(f(z)) & = \frac{2xy(x - 1) - (x^2 - y^2 + 1)y}{(x - 1)^2 + y^2}. \end{align*}
  5. For \( f(z) = \vert z \vert \bar{z} \): \[ \vert z \vert = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}, \text{ and } \bar{z} = x - \iota y. \] Therefore, \[ f(z) = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}(x - \iota y) = x\sqrt{x^2 + y^2} - \iota y\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}. \] Thus,
    \begin{align*} \text{Re} (f(z)) & = x\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}, \\ \text{Im} (f(z)) & = -y\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}. \end{align*}

problems.title: An Entire Doubly Periodic Function is Bounded
problems.problem:
Prove that a nonconstant entire function cannot satisfy the two equations
  1. $f(z + 1) = f(z)$
  2. \( f(z + \iota) = f(z) \)
for all \( z \in \mathbb{C} \), then \( f \) must be bounded and then Liouville's theorem will imply that it is constant.
problems.hint:
1. Use the given functional equations to conclude that \( f \) is doubly periodic with periods \( 1 \) and \( \iota \).
  2. Show that $f$ is bounded and apply Liouville's Theorem to conclude that a bounded entire function must be constant.
problems.solution:
We will prove that if the function \( f \) satisfies the given two conditions
  1. \( f(z + 1) = f(z) \)
  2. \( f(z + \iota) = f(z) \)
for all \( z \in \mathbb{C} \), then \( f \) must be bounded and then Liouville's Theorem will imply that it is constant.
First, note that the conditions imply that \( f \) is periodic with periods \( 1 \) and \( \iota \). Consider the square formed by the periods \( 1 \) and \( \iota \) in the complex plane. The function \( f \) takes the same values at all points inside this square that are equivalent modulo the periods. Therefore, \( f \) is completely determined by its values inside this square. If $S$ is the square of side length $1$, then we have $f(\mathbb{C} ) = f(S)$. As $f$ is continuous and $S$ is compact, so the image must be compact and hence bounded.
Since \( f \) is entire, it is analytic everywhere in the complex plane. By Liouville's theorem, a bounded entire function must be constant. To apply Liouville's theorem, we need to show that \( f \) is bounded. Hence, a nonconstant entire function cannot satisfy both \( f(z + 1) = f(z) \) and \( f(z + \iota) = f(z) \) for all \( z \in \mathbb{C} \).

problems.title: An Entire Function Bounded by $|z|^3/2$ is a Linear Polynomial
problems.problem:
Suppose $f$ is an entire function such that
\[
    \vert f(z) \vert \leq A + B \vert z \vert ^{3 / 2},
\]
for some $A, B \in \mathbb{R} $. Show that $f$ is a linear polynomial.
problems.hint:
1. Write the expansion of the function using Taylor series.
  2. Use the given bound condition and the Cauchy's estimate to show that the coefficients of the Taylor series expansion are zero for $n\geq 2$.
problems.solution: Given that $f$ is an entire function, so it can be represented by its Taylor series expansion around $z = 0 $. Let \begin{equation}\label{eq:25Feb2025-1} f(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n z^n \end{equation} be the Taylor series of $f$ on an open disc $\vert z \vert < r$, where \[ a_n = \frac{1}{2\pi \iota } \oint_{\vert z \vert = r} \frac{f(w)}{w^{n+1}} \mathrm{d} w = \frac{f^{(n)}(0)}{n!}. \] Since $\vert f(z) \vert \leq A + B \vert z \vert ^{3 / 2}$, on the circle $\vert z \vert = r$, the function is bounded by \[ \vert f(z) \vert \leq A + B r^{3 / 2} \coloneqq M. \] Therefore, using Cauchy's estimate, we get \[ \left\vert a_n \right\vert = \left\vert \frac{f^{(n)}(0)}{n!} \right\vert \leq \left\vert \left( \frac{n!}{r^n} M\right) \times \frac{1}{n!} \right\vert = \frac{M}{r^n}. \] Note that since $A, B$ are fixed real numbers, we can always choose $r>0$ such that $M \leq r^2$. Thus, for $n\geq 2$, \[ \lim_{r \to \infty} \frac{M}{r^n} = 0. \] Therefore, for $n\geq 2$, we have $a_n = 0$. Thus, the Taylor series expansion of $f$ in \eqref{eq:25Feb2025-1} reduces to \[ f(z) = a_0 + a_1 z. \] Thus, $f$ is a linear polynomial.

problems.title: Find all Complex Numbers z Satisfying Equations Like z³ = 1, ( (z - 1)/(z + 1) )² = 2i
problems.problem:
Find all $z \in \mathbb{C} $ such that
  1. $z^3 = 1$.
  2. $\left( \frac{z - 1}{z + 1} \right)^2 = 2 \iota $.
  3. $z^2 = 24 \iota - 7$.
  4. $z^3 = \iota - 1$.
  5. $z^4 = -1$.
problems.hint:
1. Take $z = r e^{\iota \theta}$ in (1), (4) and (5), and write the given equation in the polar form. Finally solve the equation.
  2. In the second part take $w = \frac{z - 1}{z + 1}$, then assume $w = \rho e^{\iota \phi }$ and solve the equation $w^2 = 2\iota$. Finally, obtained value of $w$ will determine the solution.
  3. In the third part take $z = x + \iota y$, and equate the real and imaginary parts to solve for $x$ and $y$.
problems.solution:
To solve this we will write $z = r e^{\iota \theta }$ ot $z = x + \iota y$.
  1. We want to find $z \in \mathbb{C} $ such that $z^3 = 1$. So, \begin{align*} z^3 = 1 & \implies \left( r e^{\iota \theta } \right) ^3 = 1 = e^{0}\\ & \implies r^3 e^{3\iota \theta } = e^0 \\ & \implies r^3 = 1 \text{ and } 3\theta = 2k\pi , k \in \mathbb{Z} \\ & \implies r = 1 \text{ and } \theta = \frac{2k\pi}{3}, \quad k = 0,1,2. \end{align*} Note that we only took three values of $k$, because for other values, the angles will repeat. Thus, the solution will be \begin{align*} z_1 & = e^0 = 1 \\ z_2 & = e^{\iota \frac{2\pi}{3} } = -\frac{1}{2} + \iota \frac{\sqrt{3} }{2}, \text{ and } \\ z_3 & = e^{\iota \frac{4\pi}{3} } = -\frac{1}{2} - \iota \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}. \end{align*}
  2. We want to solve $\left( \frac{z - 1}{z + 1} \right)^2 = 2 \iota $. Let $w = \frac{z - 1}{z + 1}$, and write $w = \rho e^{\iota \phi }$. Then we want to solve \begin{align*} w^2 = 2\iota & \implies \rho ^2 e^{2\iota \phi } = 2 e^{\iota \pi /2} \\ & \implies \rho = \sqrt{2} \text{ and } 2\phi = 2k\pi + \frac{\pi}{2}, \quad k = 0,1 \\ & \implies \rho = \sqrt{2} \text{ and } \phi = k\pi + \frac{\pi }{4}, \quad k = 0,1. \\ & \implies w_0 = \sqrt{2} e^{\iota \pi /4} \text{ and } w_1 = \sqrt{2} e^{\iota 5\pi /4} \\ & \implies w_0 = 1 + \iota \text{ and } w_1 = -1 - \iota . \end{align*} Now let $z = x + \iota y$. Then \begin{align*} \frac{z - 1}{z + 1} = w_0 & \implies \frac{x + \iota y - 1}{ x + \iota y + 1} = 1 + \iota \\ & \implies x + \iota y - 1 = x + \iota y + 1 + \iota x - y + \iota \\ & \implies 2 - y + \iota (x + 1) = 0 \\ & \implies x = -1 \text{ and } y = 2. \end{align*} Thus, \[ z_0 = -1 + 2\iota . \] Similarly, \begin{align*} \frac{z - 1}{z + 1} = -1 - \iota & \implies x + \iota y - 1 = -x - \iota y - 1 - \iota x + y - \iota \\ & \implies x - 1 = -x + y - 1 \text{ and } y = -y -x - 1\\ & \implies 2x - y = 0 \text{ and } 2y + x - 1 = 0 \\ & \implies x = -\frac{1}{5} \text{ and } y = -\frac{2}{5}. \end{align*} Thus, \[ z_1 = \frac{-1 - 2 \iota }{5}. \]
  3. We want to solve $z^2 = 24 \iota - 7$. Take $z = x + \iota y$. Then \begin{align*} (x + \iota y)^2 = 24 \iota - 7 & \implies x^2 - y^2 + \iota 2xy = 24 \iota - 7 \\ & \implies \left\{ \begin{array}{c} x^2 - y^2 = -7 \\ 2xy = 24 \\ \end{array} \right. \\ & \implies \left\{ \begin{array}{c} x^2 - y^2 = -7 \\[1ex] y = \dfrac{12}{x} \end{array} \right. \end{align*} Then substituting $y = \frac{12}{x}$ in the first equation yields, \begin{align*} x^2 - \left( \frac{12}{x} \right) ^2 + 7 = 0 & \implies x^4 - 144 + 7x^2 = 0 \\ & \implies \left( x^2 - 9 \right) \left( x^2 + 16 \right) = 0 \\ & \implies x = \pm 3 \quad (\text{ since } x \in \mathbb{R} ). \end{align*} Therefore, \[ y = \pm 4 \text{ and } z = \pm 3 \pm 4\iota . \]
  4. We want to solve $z^3 = \iota - 1$. Take $z = r e^{\iota \theta }$. Note that $\iota - 1 = \sqrt{2} e^{\iota \frac{3\pi}{4}}$. Thus, \begin{align*} z^3 = \iota - 1 & \implies r^3 e^{\iota 3\theta } = \sqrt{2} e^{\iota \frac{3\pi}{4}} \\ & \implies r^3 = \sqrt{2} \text{ and } e^{\iota 3\theta } = e^{\iota 3\pi /4} \\ & \implies r = \sqrt[6]{2} \text{ and } 3\theta = 2k\pi + 3\pi /4, \quad k = 0,1,2 \\ & \implies r = \sqrt[6]{2} \text{ and } \theta = \frac{2k\pi}{3} + \frac{\pi}{4}, \quad k = 0,1,2. \end{align*} Therefore, \begin{align*} z_0 & = \sqrt[6]{2} e^{\iota \frac{\pi}{4}} , \quad z_1 = \sqrt[6]{2} e^{\iota \left(\frac{11\pi}{12}\right)} \text{ and } z_2 = \sqrt[6]{2} e^{\iota \left(\frac{19\pi}{12}\right)}. \end{align*}
  5. We want to solve $z^4 = -1$. Take $z = r e^{\iota \theta }$. Then, \begin{align*} z^4 = -1 & \implies r^4 e^{\iota 4 \theta } = e^{\iota \pi} \\ & \implies r^4 = 1 \text{ and } 4\theta = \pi + 2k\pi, \quad k \in \mathbb{Z} \\ & \implies r = 1 \text{ and } \theta = \frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{k\pi}{2}, \quad k = 0, 1, 2, 3. \end{align*} Thus, \begin{align*} z_0 & = e^{\iota \frac{\pi}{4}} = \frac{1 + \iota }{\sqrt{2} } \\ z_1 & = e^{\iota \frac{3\pi}{4}} = \frac{-1 + \iota }{\sqrt{2} } \\ z_2 & = e^{\iota \frac{5\pi}{4}} = \frac{-1 - \iota }{\sqrt{2} } \\ z_3 & = e^{\iota \frac{7\pi}{4}} = \frac{-1 + \iota }{\sqrt{2} }. \end{align*}

problems.title: Complex Integration Over Piecewise Broken Paths
problems.problem:
Compute the integral
\[
    \int_\gamma \vert z \vert \mathrm{d} z,
\]
where $\gamma $ is the curve defined by
\[
    \gamma (t) =
    \begin{cases}
        3e^{\iota t},  & t\in \left[ 0, \frac{\pi}{2} \right],\\[1ex]
        \iota \left( 3 + \frac{\pi}{2} - t  \right), & t \in \left[ \frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}+3   \right] ,\\[1ex]
        t - \frac{\pi}{2} - 3, & \left[ \frac{\pi}{2} + 3, \frac{\pi}{2} + 6   \right] .
    \end{cases}
\]
problems.hint: Draw the curve and note that it is same as \[ \eta (t) = \begin{cases} 3e^{\iota t}, & t\in \left[ 0, \frac{\pi}{2} \right],\\[1ex] \iota t, & t \in \left[ 3, 0 \right] ,\\[1ex] t, & \left[ 0,3 \right] . \end{cases} \]
problems.solution:
Note that \[ \gamma (t) = \begin{cases} 3e^{\iota t}, & t\in \left[ 0, \frac{\pi}{2} \right],\\[1ex] \iota \left( 3 + \frac{\pi}{2} - t \right), & t \in \left[ \frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}+3 \right] ,\\[1ex] t - \frac{\pi}{2} - 3, & \left[ \frac{\pi}{2} + 3, \frac{\pi}{2} + 6 \right] . \end{cases} \] is same as \[ \eta (t) = \begin{cases} 3e^{\iota t}, & t\in \left[ 0, \frac{\pi}{2} \right],\\[1ex] \iota t, & t \in \left[ 3,0 \right] ,\\[1ex] t, & \left[ 0,3 \right] . \end{cases} \] Let \begin{align*} \gamma _1(t) & = 3e^{\iota t}, \quad t \in \left[ 0, \frac{\pi }{2} \right] \\[1ex] \gamma _2(t) & = \iota t, \quad t \in \left[3, 0 \right] \\[1ex] \gamma _3(t) & = t, \quad t \in [0,3]. \end{align*}
Thus, \begin{align*} \int_\gamma \vert z \vert \mathrm{d} z & = \int _{\gamma_1 \cup \gamma _2 \cup \gamma _3} \vert z \vert \mathrm{d}z \\ & = \int_{\gamma _1} \left\vert \gamma _1(t) \right\vert \gamma _1'(t) \mathrm{d} t + \int_{\gamma _2} \left\vert \gamma _2(t) \right\vert \gamma _2'(t) \mathrm{d} t \\ & \kern 2cm + \int_{\gamma _3} \left\vert \gamma _3(t) \right\vert \gamma _3'(t) \mathrm{d} t \\[1ex] & = \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} 3 \cdot 3\iota e^{\iota t}\mathrm{d} t + \int_3^0 t \iota \mathrm{d} t + \int_0^3 t \mathrm{d} t \\[1ex] & = 9\iota \int_0^{\frac{\pi }{2}} (\cos t - \iota \sin t)\mathrm{d} t + (1-\iota ) \int _0^3 t\mathrm{d} t\\ & = 9\iota \left[ \sin t + \iota \cos t \right]_0^{\pi /2} + (1 - \iota ) \left[ \frac{t^2}{2} \right]_0^3 \\ & = -\frac{9}{2} + \frac{9}{2}\iota . \end{align*} Thus, \[ \textcolor{blue}{ \boxed{ \int_{\gamma }\vert z \vert \mathrm{d} z = -\frac{9}{2} + \frac{9}{2}\iota } } \]

problems.title: Find Harmonic Conjugate of $u(x,y) = x^3 - 3xy^2 - 2y$
problems.problem: Let $u(x,y) = x^3 - 3xy^2 - 2y $. Prove that $u$ is harmonic and find a analytic function $f$ such that $\text{ Re } (f) = u$ and $f(0) = 0$.
problems.hint:
1. A function $u$ is harmonic if \[ \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = 0. \]
  2. To find the harmonic conjugate, use either Cauchy-Riemann equations to find $v$ or use Milne-Thomson's method to find $f(z)$ which is given by \[ f(z) = u(z,0) - \iota \int \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} (z,0) \ \mathrm{d} z. \]
problems.solution:
To prove that \( u(x, y) \) is harmonic, we need to show that it satisfies Laplace's equation: \[ \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = 0. \] At first, compute the partial derivatives of \( u(x, y) \) which gives \[ \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 3x^2 - 3y^2, \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = -6xy - 2. \] Now, compute the second partial derivatives, we get \[ \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = 6x, \quad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = -6x. \] Adding these, \[ \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = 6x - 6x = 0. \] Thus, \( u(x, y) \) is harmonic.
Next, we find an analytic function \( f(z) = u(x, y) + \iota v(x, y) \), where \( z = x + \iota y \), such that \( \text{Re}(f) = u \). Recall that as $f$ is analytic, it must satisfy the Cauchy-Riemann equations, that is, \[ \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}, \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = -\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}. \] Using the Cauchy-Riemann equations: \[ \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} = 3x^2 - 3y^2, \quad \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} = 6xy + 2. \] Therefore, \begin{align*} v(x, y) = \int (3x^2 - 3y^2) \ \mathrm{d} y = 3x^2 y - y^3 + h(x), \end{align*} where \( h(x) \) is a function of \( x \) alone.
Differentiate \( v(x, y) \) with respect to \( x \) and equate to \( \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} \): \begin{align*} \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} = 6xy + h'(x) & \implies 6xy + 2 = 6xy + h'(x) \\ & \implies h'(x) = 2 \implies h(x) = 2x + C, \end{align*} where \( C \) is a constant. Therefore, \[ v(x, y) = 3x^2y - y^3 + 2x + C. \] So, the analytic function will be \begin{align*} f(z) & = u(x, y) + \iota v(x, y) \\ & = (x^3 - 3xy^2 - 2y) + \iota (3x^2y - y^3 + 2x + C). \end{align*} Using the condition \( f(0) = 0 \), we find \( C = 0 \). Therefore: \[ \textcolor{blue}{ \boxed{ f(z) = (x^3 - 3xy^2 - 2y) + \iota (3x^2y - y^3 + 2x) } } \]

Method 2: Milne-Thomson's Method

We could have used the Milne-Thomson's method to construct an analytic function \( f(z) \) from the real part \( u(x,y) \). Using Milne-Thomson's method, we construct the analytic function \( f(z) \) from the real part \( u(x, y) \) as follows: \begin{align*} f(z) & = u(z,0) - \iota \int \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} (z,0) \ \mathrm{d} z \\ & = \left( z^3 - 0 - 0 \right) - \iota \int (-0 - 2)\ \mathrm{d} z \\ & = z^3 + 2\iota z + C. \end{align*} Using the condition \( f(0) = 0 \), we get \( C = 0 \). Thus, the analytic function is \[ \textcolor{blue}{ \boxed{ f(z) = z^3 - 2\iota z } } \]

problems.title: Prove that if $f$ is analytic and non-constant on a compact domain, $\text{ Re }f$ and $\text{ Im } f$ assume their maxima and minima on the boundary.
problems.problem: Show that if $f$ is analytic and non-constant on a compact domain, $\text{ Re }f$ and $\text{ Im } f$ assume their maxima and minima on the boundary.
problems.hint:
1. Consider the function $e^{f(z)}$ and $e^{-\iota f(z)}$.
  2. Apply the maximum and minimum modulus theorem to the above functions.
problems.solution: Let $f: K \to \mathbb{C} $ be a non-constant analytic function on $K$, where $K$ is a compact set. We will show that $\text{Re } f$ and $\text{Im } f$ attain their maxima and minima on the boundary of $K$. Consider the functions $e^{f(z)}$ and $e^{-\iota f(z)}$. Since $f$ is non-constant analytic on $K$, the functions $e^{f(z)}$ and $e^{-\iota f(z)}$ must be non-constant analytic on $K$. Also note that both functions are nonzero on $K$. Thus we can apply Maximum Modulus Theorem and Minimum Modulus Theorem (being nonzero is needed for minimum modulus theorem) to $e^{f(z)}$ and $e^{-\iota f(z)}$ to conclude that they attain their maxima and minima on the boundary of $\partial K$. Let $z_1, z_2 \in \partial K$ be such that for any $z \in K$ \begin{align*} & \left\vert e^{f(z)} \right\vert \leq \left\vert e^{f(z_1)} \right\vert \quad \text{ and } \quad \left\vert e^{f(z)} \right\vert \geq \left\vert e^{f(z_2)} \right\vert \\ \implies & e^{\text{Re }f(z)} \leq e^{\text{Re }f(z_1)} \quad \text{ and } \quad e^{\text{Re } f(z)} \geq \ e^{\text{Re } f(z_2)} \end{align*} Combining with the fact that $e^x$ is an increasing function on $R$, we conclude that $\text{Re } f$ attains its maxima and minima on the boundary of $K$. Similarly, since \[ \left\vert e^{-\iota f(z)} \right\vert = e^{\text{Im } f(z)}, \] we can conclude that $\text{Im } f$ attains its maxima and minima on the boundary of $K$.

problems.title: Given |z - 5 - 3i| = 3, sketch the locus of P, find its Cartesian equation, and determine the maximum value of arg(z) in (-π, π)
problems.problem:
A complex number $z$ is represented by the point $O$ in the Argand diagram. Given that $\vert z - 5 - 3\iota \vert = 3$,
  1. sketch the locus of $P$ ;
  2. find the Cartesian equation of this locus;
  3. find the maximum value of $\arg z$ in the interval $(-\pi ,\pi )$.
problems.hint:
1. The equation $\vert z - z_0 \vert = r$, denotes a circle with center $z_0$ and radius $r$.
  2. To find the maximum value of $\arg z$, consider the triangle formed by the tangent lines from the origin and find the angle.
problems.solution:
We take $z = x + \iota y$.
  1. The locus of point $P$ satisfying the equation \( \vert z - 5 - 3\iota \vert = 3 \) is a circle centered at the point \( (5, 3) \) with a radius of \( 3 \).
  2. The Cartesian equation of the locus can be obtained by squaring both sides of the equation: \begin{align*} \vert z - 5 - 3 \iota \vert = 3 & \implies \vert x + \iota y - 5 - 3 \iota \vert = 5 \\ & \implies \sqrt{(x-5)^2 + (y - 3)^2} = 3 \\ & \implies (x - 5)^2 + (y - 3)^2 = 9. \end{align*}
  3. To find the maximum value of $\arg z$, consider the following picture.
    The maximum value of $\arg z$ occurs when the line between the origin and $P$ is a tangent to the circle. Now we need to find the angle $\theta $ in the figure. Note that both the triangles $\triangle OAC$ and $\triangle OBC$ are congruent (by RHS congruence criterion). Thus, both the angles are same, which is denoted by $\theta $. Use triangle $OBC$, to get \begin{align*} \tan \theta = \frac{BC}{OB} & = \frac{3}{5} \implies \theta \tan ^{-1} \left( \frac{3}{5} \right) . \end{align*} Thus, the maximum value of $\arg z$ is equals to $\tan ^{-1} \left( \frac{3}{5} \right)$.

problems.title: Show that the integral of f(z) = z³ / (z² + 7z + 12) around the unit circle centered at the origin is zero
problems.problem:
Let
\[
    f(z) = \frac{z^3}{z^2 + 7z + 12}.
\]
Show that
\[
    \int_{C} f(z) \ \mathrm{d} z = 0,
\]
where $C$ is the unit circle centered at at origin.
problems.hint: 1. Apply the Cauchy's Integral Theorem on the given function.
problems.solution: Given that the function is \[ f(z) = \frac{z^3}{z^2 + 7z + 12} = \frac{z^3}{(z + 4)(z+3)}. \] The function is analytic everywhere except the points $z = -4,-3$ which are not inside the unit circle. Thus, by the Cauchy's integral theorem, the given integral will be zero, that is, \[ \int_{C} f(z) \ \mathrm{d} z = 0. \]

problems.title: Show that if a function is analytic on the closed unit disk, there exists a positive integer n such that f(1/n) ≠ 1/(n+1)
problems.problem: Show that if $f$ is analytic in $\vert z \vert \leq 1$, there must be some positive integer $n$ such that $f\left( \frac{1}{n} \right) \neq \frac{1}{n+1} $.
problems.hint:
1. If such a function exists, then consider the function \[ g(z) \coloneqq f(z) - \frac{z}{z + 1}, \quad \vert z \vert < 1. \]
  2. Apply the identity theorem on the unit disc.
problems.solution: Suppose that for every $n \in \mathbb{N} $, $f\left( \frac{1}{n} \right) = \frac{1}{n+1} $. Consider the function \[ g(z) \coloneqq f(z) - \frac{z}{z + 1}, \quad \vert z \vert < 1. \] Since $f$ is analytic in the unit disc, and $\frac{z}{1 + z}$ is also analytic on the unit disc, so $g$ is analytic in $\vert z \vert < 1$. For any $n\in \mathbb{N} $, we have \begin{align*} g\left( \frac{1}{n} \right) & = f\left( \frac{1}{n} \right) - \frac{\frac{1}{n}}{1+ \frac{1}{n}} \\ & = \frac{1}{n+1} - \frac{1}{n+1} = 0. \end{align*} Since the sequence $\left( \frac{1}{n} \right) $ converges to $ 0 \in D(0,1) = \{ z: \vert z \vert < 1 \} $, therefore, by the uniqueness theorem (identity theorem), we have \[ g \equiv 0 \implies f(z) = \frac{z}{1 + z}, \quad z \in D(0,1). \] Since $f$ is given to be analytic in the closed unit disc $\overline{D(0,1)} $, so the above function should be continuous at $z = -1 \in \overline{D(0,1)} $. But note that for any sequence $\left( z_n \right) $ converging to $-1$, \begin{align*} \lim_{n \to \infty} f\left( z_n \right) = \frac{z_n}{1 - z_n}, \end{align*} which does not exist. Hence, no such analytic function exists.

problems.title: Prove that if f satisfies |f(x) - f(y)| ≤ (x - y)², then f is Constant
problems.problem: Let $f$ be analytic in the closed unit disk $|z| \leq 1$. Show that there exists some positive integer $n$ such that $f\left( \frac{1}{n} \right) \neq \frac{1}{n^2 + 1}$.
problems.hint:
1. Consider the function \[g(z) \coloneqq f(z) - \frac{1}{z^2 + 1}, \quad |z| \lt 1.\]
  2. Use identity theorem to conclude that $g(z) \equiv 0$ for $|z| \lt 1$ and hence $f(z) = \frac{1}{z^2 + 1}$.
problems.solution:
Suppose, for contradiction, that $f\left( \frac{1}{n} \right) = \frac{1}{n^2 + 1}$ for all positive integers $n$. Define a function \[ g(z) \coloneqq f(z) - \frac{1}{z^2 + 1}, \quad |z| < 1. \] Since $f$ is analytic in $|z| \leq 1$, and the function $\frac{1}{z^2 + 1}$ is analytic in the open unit disk $|z| < 1$ (its poles are at $z = \pm i$, which lie on $|z| = 1$), it follows that $g$ is analytic in $|z| < 1$. Evaluating $g$ at the points $z = \frac{1}{n}$, we have \begin{align*} g\left( \frac{1}{n} \right) & = f\left( \frac{1}{n} \right) - \frac{1}{\left( \frac{1}{n} \right)^2 + 1} \\ & = \frac{1}{n^2 + 1} - \frac{1}{\frac{1}{n^2} + 1} \\ & = \frac{1}{n^2 + 1} - \frac{1}{\frac{1 + n^2}{n^2}} \\ & = \frac{1}{n^2 + 1} - \frac{n^2}{n^2 + 1} = 0. \end{align*} Thus, $g\left( \frac{1}{n} \right) = 0$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Since the sequence $\left( \frac{1}{n} \right)$ converges to $0$, which lies in the open unit disk $|z| < 1$, and $0$ is a limit point of the sequence, the identity theorem for analytic functions implies that $g(z) \equiv 0$ in $|z| < 1$. Hence, \[ f(z) = \frac{1}{z^2 + 1}, \quad |z| < 1. \]
However, $f$ is given to be analytic in the closed unit disk $|z| \leq 1$, which includes the boundary $|z| = 1$. The function $\frac{1}{z^2 + 1}$ has poles at $z = \pm i$, where $|z| = |i| = 1$, and these points lie on the boundary of the closed unit disk. So, the function can not be analytic on $\overline{D(0,1)} $ which contradicts the assumption that $f$ is analytic in $|z| \leq 1$. Therefore, the assumption that $f\left( \frac{1}{n} \right) = \frac{1}{n^2 + 1}$ for all $n$ is impossible. Hence, there must exist some positive integer $n$ such that $f\left( \frac{1}{n} \right) \neq \frac{1}{n^2 + 1}$.

problems.title: Solve $z^2 + (2\iota - 3)z + (5 - \iota) = 0$
problems.problem: Solve the quadratic equation $z^2 + (2\iota - 3)z + (5 - \iota) = 0$.
problems.hint: • Use the quadratic formula. To find $\sqrt{-15 - 8\iota}$, solve $(a + \iota b)^2 = -15 - 8\iota$ using also $a^2 + b^2 = |-15 - 8\iota| = 17$.
problems.solution:
The discriminant is $\Delta = (2\iota - 3)^2 - 4(5 - \iota) = (5 - 12\iota) - (20 - 4\iota) = -15 - 8\iota$.
Square root of $\Delta$. If $(a + \iota b)^2 = -15 - 8\iota$, then $a^2 - b^2 = -15$, $2ab = -8$, and $a^2 + b^2 = |\Delta| = 17$. So $a^2 = 1$, $b^2 = 16$, and $ab \lt 0$: $\sqrt{\Delta} = \pm(1 - 4\iota)$.
Roots. \[ z = \frac{(3 - 2\iota) \pm (1 - 4\iota)}{2} = 2 - 3\iota \quad \text{or} \quad 1 + \iota. \] Check: the sum of the roots is $3 - 2\iota = -(2\iota - 3)$ and the product is $(2 - 3\iota)(1 + \iota) = 2 + 2\iota - 3\iota + 3 = 5 - \iota$, as required by Vieta's formulas.

problems.title: When does equality hold in the triangle inequality $\vert z_1 + z_2 \vert \leq \vert z_1 \vert + \vert z_2 \vert$?
problems.problem: Prove that $|z_1 + z_2| = |z_1| + |z_2|$ if and only if one of $z_1, z_2$ is a nonnegative real multiple of the other.
problems.hint: • Expand $|z_1 + z_2|^2 = |z_1|^2 + |z_2|^2 + 2\operatorname{Re}(z_1\overline{z_2})$ and compare with $(|z_1| + |z_2|)^2$.
problems.solution:
We have $|z_1 + z_2|^2 = |z_1|^2 + |z_2|^2 + 2\operatorname{Re}(z_1\overline{z_2})$ and $(|z_1| + |z_2|)^2 = |z_1|^2 + |z_2|^2 + 2|z_1\overline{z_2}|$. So equality holds iff \[ \operatorname{Re}(z_1\overline{z_2}) = |z_1\overline{z_2}|, \] i.e. iff $z_1\overline{z_2}$ is a nonnegative real number $t$ (a complex number whose real part equals its modulus is real and $\geq 0$).
If $z_2 = 0$ the condition holds and $z_2 = 0 \cdot z_1$. If $z_2 \neq 0$, then $z_1 = \frac{z_1\overline{z_2}}{|z_2|^2} z_2 = \frac{t}{|z_2|^2}z_2$, a nonnegative multiple of $z_2$. Conversely, if $z_1 = s z_2$ with $s \geq 0$, then $z_1\overline{z_2} = s|z_2|^2 \geq 0$. Geometrically: equality holds exactly when the vectors $z_1$ and $z_2$ point in the same direction.

problems.title: An equilateral triangle criterion: $z_1^2 + z_2^2 + z_3^2 = z_1z_2 + z_2z_3 + z_3z_1$
problems.problem:
Show that three distinct complex numbers $z_1, z_2, z_3$ are the vertices of an equilateral triangle if and only if
    \[
        z_1^2 + z_2^2 + z_3^2 = z_1z_2 + z_2z_3 + z_3z_1.
    \]
problems.hint: • With $\omega = e^{2\pi\iota/3}$, the triangle $z_1z_2z_3$ is equilateral and positively oriented iff $z_1 + \omega z_2 + \omega^2 z_3 = 0$. Multiply $(z_1 + \omega z_2 + \omega^2 z_3)(z_1 + \omega^2 z_2 + \omega z_3)$.
problems.solution:
Let $\omega = e^{2\pi\iota/3}$, so $\omega^3 = 1$ and $1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 0$. Note $e^{\iota\pi/3} = -\omega^2$.
Orientation. The triangle $z_1 z_2 z_3$ is equilateral and counterclockwise iff $z_3 - z_1 = e^{\iota\pi/3}(z_2 - z_1) = -\omega^2(z_2 - z_1)$, i.e. $z_3 = (1 + \omega^2)z_1 - \omega^2 z_2 = -\omega z_1 - \omega^2 z_2$, i.e. $\omega z_1 + \omega^2 z_2 + z_3 = 0$; multiplying by $\omega^2$, iff \[ z_1 + \omega z_2 + \omega^2 z_3 = 0. \] Similarly it is equilateral and clockwise iff $z_1 + \omega^2 z_2 + \omega z_3 = 0$.
The identity. Using $\omega^3 = 1$ and $\omega + \omega^2 = -1$, \[ (z_1 + \omega z_2 + \omega^2 z_3)(z_1 + \omega^2 z_2 + \omega z_3) = z_1^2 + z_2^2 + z_3^2 - z_1z_2 - z_2z_3 - z_3z_1. \] So the right side vanishes iff one of the two factors vanishes, i.e. iff the triangle is equilateral (with one of the two orientations).

problems.title: Automorphisms of the Extended Complex Plane are Möbius Transformations
problems.problem: Let $\bar{\mathbb{C}} = \mathbb{C}  \cup \{ \infty  \} $ be the extended complex plane. Show that every automorphism of the extended complex plane is a Möbius transformation.
problems.solution: I encourage you to attempt to solve the problem today. The solution will be provided tomorrow. This will give you the opportunity to test your understanding of the problem and to improve your skills in solving similar problems in the future.

problems.title: A Function satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann Equations but not Differentiable
problems.problem:
Suppose that $z = x + \iota y$ and define a function
\[
    f(z) =
    \begin{cases}
        \frac{x^2 - y^2 - 2xy \iota }{x + \iota y}, &\text{ if } z \neq 0 ;\\
        0, &\text{ if } \text{ otherwise}.
    \end{cases}
\]
Show that $f$ satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann equations at $z = 0$, but it is not differentiable at $z = 0$.
problems.hint:
1. Note that $\bar{z}^2 = x^2 - y^2 - 2xy \iota$. Expand the function in $x,y$ and write $f(z) = u(x,y) + \iota v(x,y)$. The cauchy-Riemann equations at $z = z_0$ are \[u_x(z_0) = v_y(z_0) \text{ and } u_y(z_0) = - v_x(z_0).\] Use the definition of partial derivatives to evaluate these limits.
  2. To check if the function is differentiable or not, consider the limit $\lim_{z \to 0} \frac{f(z) - f(0)}{z}$ and evaluate the limit in two different directions.
problems.solution:
The given function is \[ f(z) = \begin{cases} \frac{x^2 - y^2 - 2xy \iota }{x + \iota y}, &\text{ if } z \neq 0 ;\\ 0, &\text{ if } \text{ otherwise}. \end{cases} \] Note that $\bar{z} ^2 = (x - \iota y)^2 = x^2 - 2xy \iota - y^2$. Thus, \begin{align*} f(z) = \begin{cases} \frac{\bar{z} ^2}{z}, &\text{ if } z\neq 0 ;\\ 0, &\text{ if } \text{ otherwise}. \end{cases} \end{align*} On of the formulation of the Cauchy-Riemann equations is $\frac{\partial f}{\partial \bar{z} } = 0 $. Note that \begin{align*} \frac{\partial f}{\partial \bar{z} } = \frac{2 \bar{z} }{z}. \end{align*} Since $\displaystyle \lim_{z \to 0} \frac{\partial f}{\partial \bar{z} } $ does not exist, and hence the function does not satisfy the Cauchy-Riemann equation at $z = 0$.
We can also solve this by writing $f = u + \iota v$. \begin{align*} f(z) & = \frac{\bar{z} ^2}{z} \times \frac{\bar{z} }{\bar{z} } = \frac{\bar{z} ^3}{\vert z \vert ^2} \\ & = \frac{(x - \iota y)^3}{x^2 + y^2} \\ & = \frac{x^3 + 3x y^2}{x^2 + y^2} + \iota \left( \frac{y^3 - 3x^2 y}{x^2 + y^2} \right). \end{align*} Thus, \[ u(x,y) = \frac{x^3 + 3x y^2}{x^2 + y^2}\quad \text{ and } \quad v(x,y) = \frac{y^3 - 3x^2 y}{x^2 + y^2}. \] Recall that the Cauchy-Riemann equations at $z_0 = (x_0, y_0)$ are \[ u_x(z_0) = v_y(z_0) \text{ and } u_y(z_0) = - v_x(z_0). \] We need to check the Cauchy-Riemann equations at $z = 0$. Note that \begin{align*} u_x(0,0) & = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{u((h,0)) - u(0,0)}{h} = \frac{h}{h} = 1\\ v_x(0,0) & = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{v((h,0)) - v(0,0)}{h} = 0\\ u_y(0,0) & = \lim_{k \to 0} \frac{u((0,k)) - u(0,0)}{k} = 0 \\ v_y(0,0) & = \lim_{k \to 0} \frac{v((0,k)) - v(0,0)}{k} = \frac{h}{h} = 1. \end{align*} Thus, $f$ satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann equations at $z = (0,0)$.
We now will check the differentiability of $f$ at $(0,0)$. Recall that $f$ is differentiable at $z = 0$ if the following limit exists \begin{align*} \lim_{z \to 0} \frac{f(z) - f(0)}{z} & = \lim_{z \to 0} \frac{\frac{\bar{z} ^2}{z} - 0}{z} \\ & \lim_{z \to 0} \frac{\bar{z} ^2}{z^2}. \end{align*} We will evaluate this limit in two different directions. Let $h \in \mathbb{R} $. \begin{align*} \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\left( \overline{h + \iota 0} \right) ^2}{(h + \iota 0)^2} = 0. \end{align*} On the other hand, \begin{align*} \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\left( \overline{h + \iota h} \right) ^2}{(h + \iota h)^2} & = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{h^2 (1 - \iota )^3}{h^2 ( 1 + \iota )^2} \\ & = \frac{(1 - \iota )^2}{(1 + \iota )^2} = -1. \end{align*} Thus, $f$ is not differentiable at $z = 0$.

problems.title: Show that no nonconstant analytic polynomial can take imaginary values only
problems.problem: Show that no nonconstant analytic polynomial can take imaginary values only.
problems.hint: 1. Note that the real part is zero and hence $p(z)= \iota v(x,y)$ for some real function $v$. Now use the Cauchy-Riemann equations to show that $p$ is constant.
problems.solution:
Let $p(z)$ be a polynomial which takes only imaginary values. We claim that $p$ is constant. Since $p$ takes only imaginary values, let $p(z) = \iota v(x,y)$. Since $p$ is analytic, it must satisfy the Cauchy-Riemann equations. Since, the real part is zero, then by Cauchy-Riemann equations, we must have \begin{equation}\label{eq:03Jun2025-1} v_x = 0 = v_y \implies v = k, \text{ a constant }. \end{equation} Thus, $p = \iota k$. Therefore, there does not exist any nonconstant polynomial which takes only imaginary values.
We can prove this is more generality. That is if $f$ is an entire function such that $\text{ Re } (f(z)) = 0$ for every $z\in \mathbb{C} $, then $f$ is constant. Since the real part of $f$ is zero, let $f(z) = \iota v(x,y)$. Define a function \[ g(z) = e^{f(z)} = e^{\iota v(x,y)} = \cos v(x,y) + \iota \sin v(x,y). \] Since $f$ is an entire function and the exponential is also an entire function, the function $g$ entire. Also, note that $g$ is bounded. Thus, $g$ is an entire function which is bounded and hence by Liouville's theorem, $g$ is constant. This implies $f$ is also constant.

problems.title: De Moivre: $\cos 5\theta = 16\cos^5\theta - 20\cos^3\theta + 5\cos\theta$, and $\cos\frac{\pi}{10}$
problems.problem:
Use De Moivre's formula to show that
    \[
        \cos 5\theta = 16\cos^5\theta - 20\cos^3\theta + 5\cos\theta,
    \]
    and deduce that $\cos^2\frac{\pi}{10} = \frac{5 + \sqrt{5}}{8}$.
problems.hint: • $\cos 5\theta = \operatorname{Re}(\cos\theta + \iota\sin\theta)^5$. Expand with the binomial theorem and replace $\sin^2\theta$ by $1 - \cos^2\theta$.
problems.solution:
Write $c = \cos\theta$, $s = \sin\theta$. By De Moivre, $\cos 5\theta + \iota\sin 5\theta = (c + \iota s)^5$. The real part of the binomial expansion is \[ \cos 5\theta = c^5 - 10c^3s^2 + 5cs^4. \] With $s^2 = 1 - c^2$: \[ c^5 - 10c^3(1 - c^2) + 5c(1 - c^2)^2 = c^5 - 10c^3 + 10c^5 + 5c - 10c^3 + 5c^5 = 16c^5 - 20c^3 + 5c. \]
$\cos\frac{\pi}{10}$. For $\theta = \frac{\pi}{10}$, $\cos 5\theta = \cos\frac{\pi}{2} = 0$ and $c \neq 0$, so $16c^4 - 20c^2 + 5 = 0$, giving \[ c^2 = \frac{20 \pm \sqrt{400 - 320}}{32} = \frac{5 \pm \sqrt{5}}{8}. \] Since $\cos\frac{\pi}{10} > \cos\frac{3\pi}{10}$ and both values are roots (both $\theta = \frac{\pi}{10}$ and $\frac{3\pi}{10}$ satisfy $\cos 5\theta = 0$), the larger root belongs to $\frac{\pi}{10}$: $\cos^2\frac{\pi}{10} = \frac{5 + \sqrt{5}}{8}$.

problems.title: The zeros of $\cosh z$ and $\sinh z$
problems.problem: Using $\cosh z = \cos(\iota z)$ and $\sinh z = -\iota\sin(\iota z)$, find all zeros of $\cosh z$ and of $\sinh z$ in $\mathbb{C}$.
problems.hint: • All zeros of $\sin$ and $\cos$ are real, because $|\sin(x + \iota y)|^2 = \sin^2 x + \sinh^2 y$ and $|\cos(x + \iota y)|^2 = \cos^2 x + \sinh^2 y$.
problems.solution:
Zeros of $\sin$ and $\cos$. With $w = x + \iota y$, $|\sin w|^2 = \sin^2 x + \sinh^2 y$, which vanishes iff $\sinh y = 0$ and $\sin x = 0$, i.e. $w = k\pi$. Similarly $|\cos w|^2 = \cos^2 x + \sinh^2 y$ vanishes iff $w = \frac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$.
Identities. $\cos(\iota z) = \frac{e^{-z} + e^{z}}{2} = \cosh z$ and $\sin(\iota z) = \frac{e^{-z} - e^{z}}{2\iota} = \iota\sinh z$.
Zeros. $\cosh z = 0 \iff \iota z = \frac{\pi}{2} + k\pi \iff z = \left( \frac{\pi}{2} + k\pi \right)\iota$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$. And $\sinh z = 0 \iff \iota z = k\pi \iff z = k\pi\iota$. So the zeros lie on the imaginary axis; $\cosh$ and $\sinh$ are periodic with period $2\pi\iota$.

problems.title: When does $\operatorname{Log}(z_1 z_2) = \operatorname{Log} z_1 + \operatorname{Log} z_2$?
problems.problem:
Let $\operatorname{Log} z = \ln|z| + \iota\operatorname{Arg} z$ with $-\pi \lt \operatorname{Arg} z \leq \pi$.
  1. Show that $\operatorname{Log}(z_1z_2) = \operatorname{Log} z_1 + \operatorname{Log} z_2 + 2k\pi\iota$ with $k \in \{ -1, 0, 1 \}$, and $k = 0$ exactly when $-\pi \lt \operatorname{Arg} z_1 + \operatorname{Arg} z_2 \leq \pi$.
  2. Give an example where $\operatorname{Log}(z_1z_2) \neq \operatorname{Log} z_1 + \operatorname{Log} z_2$, and show that $\operatorname{Log}(z^2) \neq 2\operatorname{Log} z$ for $z = -1$.
problems.hint: • $\ln|z_1z_2| = \ln|z_1| + \ln|z_2|$ always; only the arguments can disagree, by a multiple of $2\pi$.
problems.solution:
(a) The real parts always agree: $\ln|z_1z_2| = \ln|z_1| + \ln|z_2|$. The number $\operatorname{Arg} z_1 + \operatorname{Arg} z_2$ is an argument of $z_1z_2$, so it differs from $\operatorname{Arg}(z_1z_2)$ by $2k\pi$. Since $\operatorname{Arg} z_1 + \operatorname{Arg} z_2 \in (-2\pi, 2\pi]$ and $\operatorname{Arg}(z_1z_2) \in (-\pi, \pi]$, we get $k \in \{ -1, 0, 1 \}$, with $k = 0$ exactly when the sum already lies in $(-\pi, \pi]$.
(b) Take $z_1 = z_2 = -1$: $\operatorname{Log}\left( (-1)(-1) \right) = \operatorname{Log} 1 = 0$, while $\operatorname{Log}(-1) + \operatorname{Log}(-1) = \iota\pi + \iota\pi = 2\pi\iota$. This is also the example $z = -1$ for $\operatorname{Log}(z^2) = 0 \neq 2\pi\iota = 2\operatorname{Log} z$. (Another example: $z_1 = z_2 = e^{3\pi\iota/4}$ gives $\operatorname{Arg}(z_1z_2) = -\frac{\pi}{2}$, while the sum of the arguments is $\frac{3\pi}{2}$.)
For the multivalued logarithm, $\log(z_1z_2) = \log z_1 + \log z_2$ does hold as an equality of sets of values.

problems.title: Wirtinger derivatives: $f$ is analytic iff $\partial f / \partial \bar{z} = 0$; $e^{\bar{z}}$ is differentiable nowhere
problems.problem:
For $f = u + \iota v$ with $u, v$ having continuous partial derivatives, define \[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial \bar{z}} = \frac{1}{2}\left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + \iota\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \right). \]
  1. Show that $\frac{\partial f}{\partial \bar{z}} = 0$ at a point iff the Cauchy-Riemann equations hold there.
  2. Show that $f(z) = e^{\bar{z}}$ is complex differentiable at no point, and that $|z|^2$ is differentiable only at $0$.
problems.hint: • Expand $\frac{1}{2}(u_x + \iota v_x + \iota u_y - v_y)$ into real and imaginary parts.
problems.solution:
(a) \[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial \bar{z}} = \frac{1}{2}\left( u_x + \iota v_x + \iota u_y - v_y \right) = \frac{1}{2}(u_x - v_y) + \frac{\iota}{2}(v_x + u_y). \] This vanishes iff $u_x = v_y$ and $u_y = -v_x$, the Cauchy-Riemann equations. (With continuous partials, $f$ is then differentiable at that point.) Informally, analytic functions are those that "do not depend on $\bar{z}$".
(b) $e^{\bar{z}} = e^{x}(\cos y - \iota\sin y)$, so $u = e^x\cos y$, $v = -e^x\sin y$, and \[ u_x - v_y = 2e^x\cos y, \qquad u_y + v_x = -2e^x\sin y. \] Both vanish only if $\cos y = \sin y = 0$, which is impossible. So the Cauchy-Riemann equations hold nowhere and $e^{\bar{z}}$ is nowhere differentiable. (Formally, $\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar{z}}e^{\bar{z}} = e^{\bar{z}} \neq 0$.) For $|z|^2 = z\bar{z}$: $\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar{z}}(z\bar{z}) = z$, which vanishes only at $z = 0$; there $|z|^2$ is differentiable with derivative $0$.

problems.title: If $f$ is analytic on a domain and $\operatorname{Re} f = (\operatorname{Im} f)^2$, then $f$ is constant
problems.problem: Let $f = u + \iota v$ be analytic on a domain (connected open set) $D$, and suppose $u = v^2$ on $D$. Prove that $f$ is constant.
problems.hint: • Differentiate $u = v^2$ and use the Cauchy-Riemann equations to get $v_x(1 + 4v^2) = 0$.
problems.solution:
From $u = v^2$: $u_x = 2vv_x$ and $u_y = 2vv_y$. The Cauchy-Riemann equations $u_x = v_y$, $u_y = -v_x$ give \[ v_y = 2vv_x, \qquad -v_x = 2vv_y = 4v^2 v_x. \] So $v_x(1 + 4v^2) = 0$, and since $1 + 4v^2 > 0$, $v_x = 0$; then $v_y = 2vv_x = 0$.
Thus $f' = u_x + \iota v_x = 2vv_x + \iota v_x = 0$ throughout $D$. A function with zero derivative on a connected open set is constant. Hence $f$ is constant.
(Geometric view: the image of $f$ lies on the parabola $u = v^2$, which contains no open set, so by the open mapping theorem $f$ must be constant.)

problems.title: $\ln(x^2 + y^2)$ is harmonic on $\mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\}$ but has no harmonic conjugate there
problems.problem:
Let $u(x, y) = \ln(x^2 + y^2)$ on $\Omega = \mathbb{C} \setminus \{ 0 \}$.
  1. Show that $u$ is harmonic on $\Omega$.
  2. Show that $u$ has no harmonic conjugate on $\Omega$.
  3. Find a harmonic conjugate of $u$ on $\mathbb{C} \setminus (-\infty, 0]$.
problems.hint: • If $v$ were a conjugate, $f = u + \iota v$ would be analytic on $\Omega$ with $f' = u_x - \iota u_y = \frac{2}{z}$. Integrate $f'$ around the unit circle.
problems.solution:
(a) $u_x = \frac{2x}{x^2 + y^2}$, $u_{xx} = \frac{2(y^2 - x^2)}{(x^2 + y^2)^2}$, and by symmetry $u_{yy} = \frac{2(x^2 - y^2)}{(x^2 + y^2)^2}$. So $u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0$ on $\Omega$.
(b) Suppose $v$ is a harmonic conjugate on $\Omega$, so $f = u + \iota v$ is analytic there. Then \[ f'(z) = u_x - \iota u_y = \frac{2(x - \iota y)}{x^2 + y^2} = \frac{2\bar{z}}{|z|^2} = \frac{2}{z}. \] Since $f$ is a primitive of $f'$ on $\Omega$, $\oint_{|z| = 1} f'(z)\, \mathrm{d}z = 0$. But $\oint_{|z| = 1} \frac{2}{z}\, \mathrm{d}z = 4\pi\iota \neq 0$. Contradiction.
(c) On the slit plane, $2\operatorname{Log} z = \ln|z|^2 + 2\iota\operatorname{Arg} z$ is analytic, so $v = 2\operatorname{Arg} z$ is a harmonic conjugate. On $\Omega$ the "conjugate" would have to be $2\arg z$, which is multivalued: going once around the origin increases it by $4\pi$. Harmonic conjugates always exist on simply connected domains, but not necessarily on others.

problems.title: A bounded harmonic function on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is constant
problems.problem: Let $u$ be harmonic on all of $\mathbb{R}^2 = \mathbb{C}$ and bounded above: $u \leq M$. Prove that $u$ is constant. (In particular every bounded harmonic function on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is constant.)
problems.hint: • $u$ has a harmonic conjugate $v$ on $\mathbb{C}$, so $f = u + \iota v$ is entire. Apply Liouville's theorem to $e^{f}$.
problems.solution:
Since $\mathbb{C}$ is simply connected, $u$ has a harmonic conjugate $v$, and $f = u + \iota v$ is entire. Then $g = e^{f}$ is entire and \[ |g| = e^{\operatorname{Re} f} = e^{u} \leq e^{M}. \] By Liouville's theorem, $g$ is constant.
Hence $0 = g' = f'e^{f}$, and as $e^{f} \neq 0$, $f' = 0$: $f$ is constant, so $u = \operatorname{Re} f$ is constant. (If instead $u$ is bounded below, apply this to $-u$.)
Some bound is really needed: $u(x, y) = x$ and $u(x, y) = e^{x}\cos y$ are nonconstant harmonic functions on $\mathbb{R}^2$, and both are unbounded above and below.

problems.title: The image of the circle $\vert z - 1 \vert = 1$ under $w = 1/z$
problems.problem: Find the image of the circle $|z - 1| = 1$ (without the point $z = 0$) under the map $w = \dfrac{1}{z}$. What is the image of the disc $|z - 1| \lt 1$?
problems.hint: • $|z - 1| = 1 \iff z\bar{z} = z + \bar{z}$. Divide by $z\bar{z}$.
problems.solution:
$|z - 1|^2 = 1 \iff z\bar{z} - z - \bar{z} + 1 = 1 \iff z\bar{z} = z + \bar{z}$. For $z \neq 0$, divide by $z\bar{z}$: \[ 1 = \frac{1}{\bar{z}} + \frac{1}{z} = \bar{w} + w = 2\operatorname{Re} w. \] So the image is the vertical line $\operatorname{Re} w = \frac{1}{2}$. (Every point of the line is attained, since $z = 1/w$.)
The disc. Similarly $|z - 1| \lt 1 \iff z\bar{z} \lt z + \bar{z} \iff 1 \lt 2\operatorname{Re} w$, so the disc maps onto the half-plane $\operatorname{Re} w > \frac{1}{2}$. (Check: $z = 1 \mapsto w = 1$.) This illustrates that a circle through the pole $z = 0$ of $1/z$ becomes a line.

problems.title: The automorphisms $e^{\iota\theta}\frac{z - a}{1 - \bar{a}z}$ map the unit disc onto itself
problems.problem: Let $|a| \lt 1$ and $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $\varphi(z) = e^{\iota\theta}\dfrac{z - a}{1 - \bar{a}z}$. Prove that $\varphi$ maps the unit disc $\mathbb{D}$ one-to-one onto itself and the unit circle onto itself, and that $\varphi(a) = 0$.
problems.hint: • Prove the identity $|1 - \bar{a}z|^2 - |z - a|^2 = (1 - |z|^2)(1 - |a|^2)$.
problems.solution:
Key identity. Expanding, \[ |1 - \bar{a}z|^2 - |z - a|^2 = 1 + |a|^2|z|^2 - |z|^2 - |a|^2 = (1 - |z|^2)(1 - |a|^2). \] For $|z| \leq 1$ the denominator $1 - \bar{a}z$ is nonzero (since $|\bar{a}z| \lt 1$).
Disc and circle. Since $1 - |a|^2 > 0$, the identity shows $|\varphi(z)| = \frac{|z - a|}{|1 - \bar{a}z|} \lt 1$ iff $|z| \lt 1$, and $= 1$ iff $|z| = 1$. So $\varphi(\mathbb{D}) \subseteq \mathbb{D}$ and $\varphi$ maps the circle into the circle; and $\varphi(a) = 0$.
Bijective. Solving $w = e^{\iota\theta}\frac{z - a}{1 - \bar{a}z}$ for $z$ gives \[ z = \frac{e^{-\iota\theta}w + a}{1 + \bar{a}e^{-\iota\theta}w} = \frac{w' + a}{1 + \bar{a}w'}, \qquad w' = e^{-\iota\theta}w, \] which is again a map of the same type (with $-a$ in place of $a$, after rotation). By the same argument it maps $\mathbb{D}$ into $\mathbb{D}$. So $\varphi$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{D}$ onto itself. By Schwarz's lemma, these are in fact all the conformal automorphisms of $\mathbb{D}$.

problems.title: The cross ratio is real iff the four points lie on a circle or a line
problems.problem:
For distinct $z_1, z_2, z_3, z_4 \in \mathbb{C}$, the cross ratio is
    \[
        (z_1, z_2, z_3, z_4) = \frac{(z_1 - z_3)(z_2 - z_4)}{(z_1 - z_4)(z_2 - z_3)}.
    \]
    Prove that $(z_1, z_2, z_3, z_4)$ is real if and only if the four points lie on a circle or on a straight line.
problems.hint: • The Möbius map $T(z) = (z, z_2, z_3, z_4)$ sends $z_2, z_3, z_4$ to $1, 0, \infty$. Möbius maps send circles and lines to circles and lines.
problems.solution:
Let $T(z) = \frac{(z - z_3)(z_2 - z_4)}{(z - z_4)(z_2 - z_3)}$. This is a Möbius transformation with $T(z_2) = 1$, $T(z_3) = 0$, $T(z_4) = \infty$, and $T(z_1) = (z_1, z_2, z_3, z_4)$.
Through three distinct points there is exactly one "generalised circle" (circle or line); let $C$ be the one through $z_2, z_3, z_4$. Möbius transformations map generalised circles onto generalised circles, so $T(C)$ is the generalised circle through $1, 0, \infty$, which is $\mathbb{R} \cup \{ \infty \}$.
Since $T$ is a bijection of the extended plane, $z_1 \in C \iff T(z_1) \in \mathbb{R} \cup \{ \infty \}$. As $z_1 \neq z_4$, $T(z_1) \neq \infty$. Hence $z_1$ lies on $C$ (the four points are concyclic or collinear) iff the cross ratio is real.
Example: $1, \iota, -1, -\iota$ lie on the unit circle, and $(1, \iota, -1, -\iota) = \frac{(2)(2\iota)}{(1 + \iota)(\iota + 1)} = \frac{4\iota}{2\iota} = 2$ is real.

problems.title: Gamelin Solution - Chapter 1 - Identify and Sketch the Set
problems.problem:
Identify and sketch the set of points satisfying:
  1. $|z - 1 - i| = 1$
  2. $1 < |2z - 6| < 2$
  3. $|z - 1|^2 + |z + 1|^2 < 8$
  4. $|z - 1| + |z + 1| \leq 2$
  5. $|z - 1| < |z|$
problems.hint:
1. The equation $|z - z_0| = r$ denotes the circle of radius $r$.
  2. Express $z = x + \iota y$ and simplify the expression to see what geometric shape it represents.
problems.solution:
We recall that the equation \[ \vert z - z_0 \vert = r, \] denotes the circle with center $z_0$ and radius $r$.
  1. The set is \begin{align*} \left\{ z \in \mathbb{C} : \vert z - 1 - \iota \vert = 1 \right\} = \{ z \in \mathbb{C} : \vert z - (1 + \iota ) = 1 \vert \} , \end{align*} which is a circle with center $1 + \iota $ and radius $1$.
  2. The set is \begin{align*} 1 < \vert 2z - 6 \vert < 2 & \implies \frac{1}{2} < \vert z - 3 \vert < 1 \\ & \implies \vert z-3 \vert> \frac{1}{2} \text{ and } \vert z - 3 \vert < 1. \end{align*}
  3. The set is \begin{align*} \vert z - 1 \vert ^2 + \vert z + 1 \vert ^2 < 8. \end{align*} Take $z=x + \iota y$. Then \begin{align*} \vert z - 1 \vert ^2 + \vert z + 1 \vert ^2 < 8 & \implies \vert (x-1) +\iota y \vert ^2 + \vert (x + 1) + \iota y \vert ^2 < 8 \\ & \implies (x-1)^2 + y^2 + (x+1)^2 + y^2 < 8 \\ & \implies 2x^2 + 2y^2 + 2 < 8 \\ & \implies x^2 + y^2 < 3. \end{align*} The above represents an open disc centered at $(0,0)$ and of radius $\sqrt{3} $.
  4. The set is \begin{align*} \vert z - 1 \vert + \vert z + 1 \vert \leq 2. \end{align*} Take $z = x + \iota y$, then from the previous part, we have \begin{align*} \sqrt{(x-1)^2 + y^2} + \sqrt{(x + 1)^2 + y^2} \leq 2. \end{align*} The above is an ellipse with interior whose foci are $(1,0)$ and $(-1,0)$. This one can also be seen geometrically that the set is the locus of all point whose sum of distance from $1$ and $-1$ is constant $2$, which is an ellipse.
  5. The set is \begin{align*} \vert z - 1 \vert < \vert z \vert . \end{align*} Take $z=x + \iota y$, then \begin{align*} \vert (x - 1) + \iota y \vert < \vert x + \iota y \vert & \implies (x-1)^2 + y^2 < x^2 + y^2 \\ & \implies -2x + 1 < 0 \\ & \implies x> -\frac{1}{2}. \end{align*}

problems.title: Gamelin Solution - Chapter 1 - Identify and Sketch the Set
problems.problem:
Identify and sketch the set of points satisfying:
  1. $|z - 1 - i| = 1$
  2. $1 < |2z - 6| < 2$
  3. $|z - 1|^2 + |z + 1|^2 < 8$
  4. $|z - 1| + |z + 1| \leq 2$
  5. $|z - 1| < |z|$
problems.solution: I encourage you to attempt to solve the problem today. The solution will be provided tomorrow. This will give you the opportunity to test your understanding of the problem and to improve your skills in solving similar problems in the future.

problems.title: The Möbius map $T(z) = \frac{3z - 4}{z - 1}$: one fixed point, and a formula for $T^n$
problems.problem:
Let $T(z) = \dfrac{3z - 4}{z - 1}$.
  1. Find the fixed points of $T$.
  2. Show that $\dfrac{1}{T(z) - 2} = \dfrac{1}{z - 2} + 1$, and deduce a formula for the $n$th iterate $T^n$.
  3. Show that $T^n(z) \to 2$ for every $z$ (with $T^n(z)$ defined).
problems.hint: • A Möbius map with a single (double) fixed point $p$ is conjugate to a translation via $z \mapsto \frac{1}{z - p}$.
problems.solution:
(a) $T(z) = z \iff 3z - 4 = z^2 - z \iff (z - 2)^2 = 0$. The only fixed point is $z = 2$ (a double fixed point), so $T$ is parabolic. (Also: the normalised matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $1$ and trace $2$.)
(b) $T(z) - 2 = \frac{3z - 4 - 2z + 2}{z - 1} = \frac{z - 2}{z - 1}$, so \[ \frac{1}{T(z) - 2} = \frac{z - 1}{z - 2} = 1 + \frac{1}{z - 2}. \] So in the coordinate $\zeta = \frac{1}{z - 2}$, $T$ is the translation $\zeta \mapsto \zeta + 1$. Iterating, $\frac{1}{T^n(z) - 2} = \frac{1}{z - 2} + n$, i.e. \[ T^n(z) = 2 + \frac{z - 2}{1 + n(z - 2)}. \]
(c) In the $\zeta$-coordinate, $\zeta + n \to \infty$, which corresponds to $z \to 2$. Explicitly, for $z \neq 2$, $T^n(z) - 2 = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{z - 2} + n} \to 0$. So every orbit converges to the fixed point $2$, but only like $\frac{1}{n}$ (not geometrically, as near an attracting fixed point of a loxodromic map).

problems.title: A conformal map of the first quadrant onto the unit disc
problems.problem: Find a one-to-one conformal map of the first quadrant $Q = \{ z : \operatorname{Re} z > 0,\ \operatorname{Im} z > 0 \}$ onto the unit disc $\mathbb{D}$.
problems.hint: • First $z \mapsto z^2$ (quadrant to upper half-plane), then the Cayley map $\zeta \mapsto \frac{\zeta - \iota}{\zeta + \iota}$ (upper half-plane to disc).
problems.solution:
Step 1. $\zeta = z^2$ doubles arguments: $z = re^{\iota\varphi}$ with $0 \lt \varphi \lt \frac{\pi}{2}$ goes to $r^2e^{2\iota\varphi}$ with $0 \lt 2\varphi \lt \pi$. So $z^2$ maps $Q$ one-to-one onto the upper half-plane $H$ (it is one-to-one on $Q$ because $z^2 = w^2$ implies $z = \pm w$, and $-w \notin Q$), and it is conformal since its derivative $2z$ does not vanish on $Q$.
Step 2. $w = \frac{\zeta - \iota}{\zeta + \iota}$ maps $H$ onto $\mathbb{D}$, because $|\zeta - \iota| \lt |\zeta + \iota|$ exactly when $\zeta$ is closer to $\iota$ than to $-\iota$, i.e. $\operatorname{Im}\zeta > 0$.
Answer. \[ w = \frac{z^2 - \iota}{z^2 + \iota}. \] For example $z = e^{\iota\pi/4}$ (on the bisector) goes to $w = 0$, and the boundary rays (positive real and positive imaginary axes) go to the unit circle.

problems.title: A conformal map of the upper half-disc onto the upper half-plane
problems.problem: Find a one-to-one conformal map of the half-disc $\{ z : |z| \lt 1,\ \operatorname{Im} z > 0 \}$ onto the upper half-plane.
problems.hint: • The Möbius map $\zeta = \frac{1 + z}{1 - z}$ sends $-1 \mapsto 0$ and $1 \mapsto \infty$; check where the diameter and the semicircle go. Then square.
problems.solution:
Step 1. Let $\zeta = \frac{1 + z}{1 - z}$. It sends $-1 \mapsto 0$, $1 \mapsto \infty$, and:
  • the diameter $-1 \lt x \lt 1$ to the positive real axis ($\frac{1 + x}{1 - x} > 0$);
  • the upper semicircle $z = e^{\iota t}$, $0 \lt t \lt \pi$, to $\frac{1 + e^{\iota t}}{1 - e^{\iota t}} = \iota\cot\frac{t}{2}$, the positive imaginary axis.
The half-disc is bounded by these two arcs, and the test point $z = \frac{\iota}{2}$ goes to $\frac{1 + \iota/2}{1 - \iota/2} = \frac{3 + 4\iota}{5}$, in the first quadrant. So $\zeta$ maps the half-disc onto the first quadrant.
Step 2. $w = \zeta^2$ maps the first quadrant onto the upper half-plane (as in the previous problem). Hence \[ w = \left( \frac{1 + z}{1 - z} \right)^2 \] maps the upper half-disc conformally onto the upper half-plane.

problems.title: Cauchy-Hadamard: the radius of convergence of $\sum (2 + (-1)^n)^n z^n$
problems.problem: Find the radius of convergence of $\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \left( 2 + (-1)^n \right)^n z^n$. Why does the ratio test not work here?
problems.hint: • $R = 1 / \limsup |a_n|^{1/n}$ (Cauchy-Hadamard).
problems.solution:
Here $|a_n|^{1/n} = 2 + (-1)^n$, which is $3$ for even $n$ and $1$ for odd $n$. Hence $\limsup |a_n|^{1/n} = 3$, and by the Cauchy-Hadamard formula \[ R = \frac{1}{3}. \]
Directly: for $|z| \lt \frac{1}{3}$, $|a_nz^n| \leq (3|z|)^n$, a convergent geometric series; for $|z| \geq \frac{1}{3}$, the even terms satisfy $|a_{2k}z^{2k}| = (3|z|)^{2k} \geq 1$, so the terms do not tend to $0$.
The ratio test fails because $\left| \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right|$ alternates between $\frac{3^{n+1}}{1}$ (for $n$ odd) and $\frac{1}{3^n}$ (for $n$ even): it has no limit, so the ratio test gives no information. The root test, through the $\limsup$, always works.

problems.title: Convergence of $\sum \frac{z^n}{n}$ on the boundary circle
problems.problem: Determine all $z \in \mathbb{C}$ for which $\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{z^n}{n}$ converges.
problems.hint: • The radius of convergence is $1$. On $|z| = 1$, $z \neq 1$, use Dirichlet's test: the partial sums of $\sum z^n$ are bounded and $\frac{1}{n}$ decreases to $0$.
problems.solution:
Inside and outside. $\left| \frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} \right| = \frac{n + 1}{n} \to 1$, so $R = 1$: the series converges (absolutely) for $|z| \lt 1$ and diverges for $|z| > 1$.
On $|z| = 1$. At $z = 1$ it is the harmonic series, which diverges. For $|z| = 1$, $z \neq 1$: \[ \left| \sum_{k=1}^{N} z^k \right| = \left| \frac{z(1 - z^N)}{1 - z} \right| \leq \frac{2}{|1 - z|} \] is bounded independently of $N$, and $\frac{1}{n}$ decreases to $0$. By Dirichlet's test (summation by parts), $\sum \frac{z^n}{n}$ converges, though not absolutely (since $\sum \frac{1}{n} = \infty$).
So the series converges exactly on $\{ |z| \leq 1 \} \setminus \{ 1 \}$. Its sum is $-\operatorname{Log}(1 - z)$ there (by Abel's theorem on the circle); for example $z = -1$ gives $\sum \frac{(-1)^n}{n} = -\ln 2$.

problems.title: The Riemann zeta function $\zeta(s) = \sum n^{-s}$ is analytic on $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$
problems.problem: Let $n^{-s} = e^{-s\ln n}$. Prove that $\zeta(s) = \displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^{-s}$ converges uniformly on each half-plane $\operatorname{Re} s \geq \sigma_0$ with $\sigma_0 > 1$, and that $\zeta$ is analytic on $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$ with $\zeta'(s) = -\sum_{n \geq 2} (\ln n)\, n^{-s}$.
problems.hint: • $|n^{-s}| = n^{-\operatorname{Re} s}$. Use the Weierstrass M-test and the theorem that a uniform limit of analytic functions is analytic.
problems.solution:
Each term $n^{-s} = e^{-s\ln n}$ is entire, and $|n^{-s}| = e^{-\operatorname{Re}(s)\ln n} = n^{-\operatorname{Re} s}$. On $\operatorname{Re} s \geq \sigma_0 > 1$, \[ |n^{-s}| \leq n^{-\sigma_0}, \qquad \sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-\sigma_0} \lt \infty. \] By the Weierstrass M-test the series converges absolutely and uniformly on this half-plane.
By Weierstrass's theorem (a locally uniform limit of analytic functions is analytic, and may be differentiated term by term; proved with Morera's theorem and Cauchy's integral formula), $\zeta$ is analytic on $\operatorname{Re} s > \sigma_0$, and \[ \zeta'(s) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}s}e^{-s\ln n} = -\sum_{n=2}^\infty (\ln n)\, n^{-s}. \] Every point with $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$ lies in such a half-plane (take $\sigma_0$ between $1$ and $\operatorname{Re} s$), so $\zeta$ is analytic on $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$. (The convergence is not uniform on all of $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$: near $s = 1$, $\zeta(s) \to \infty$.)

problems.title: Maximum of $\vert z^2 + 3z - 1 \vert$ on the closed unit disc
problems.problem: Find the maximum value of $|z^2 + 3z - 1|$ on the closed disc $|z| \leq 1$, and the points where it is attained.
problems.hint: • By the maximum modulus principle the maximum is on $|z| = 1$. With $z = e^{\iota\theta}$, factor out $e^{\iota\theta}$.
problems.solution:
By the maximum modulus principle, the maximum over $|z| \leq 1$ of the modulus of the (nonconstant) polynomial is attained on the circle $|z| = 1$.
For $z = e^{\iota\theta}$, \[ |z^2 + 3z - 1| = |e^{\iota\theta}| \cdot \left| e^{\iota\theta} + 3 - e^{-\iota\theta} \right| = |3 + 2\iota\sin\theta| = \sqrt{9 + 4\sin^2\theta}. \] This is largest when $\sin\theta = \pm 1$, i.e. $z = \pm\iota$.
Hence the maximum is $\sqrt{13}$, attained exactly at $z = \iota$ and $z = -\iota$. (Check: $\iota^2 + 3\iota - 1 = -2 + 3\iota$, of modulus $\sqrt{13}$.)

problems.title: The residue of $\frac{e^{1/z}}{1 - z}$ at $z = 0$ is $e - 1$
problems.problem: Find the residue of $f(z) = \dfrac{e^{1/z}}{1 - z}$ at its essential singularity $z = 0$. Hence evaluate $\displaystyle \oint_{|z| = 1/2} f(z)\, \mathrm{d}z$ and $\displaystyle \oint_{|z| = 2} f(z)\, \mathrm{d}z$.
problems.hint: • Multiply the Laurent series $e^{1/z} = \sum_{k \geq 0} \frac{z^{-k}}{k!}$ and $\frac{1}{1 - z} = \sum_{m \geq 0} z^m$ (valid for $0 \lt |z| \lt 1$) and collect the coefficient of $z^{-1}$.
problems.solution:
For $0 \lt |z| \lt 1$ both series converge absolutely, so their product can be rearranged: \[ f(z) = \sum_{k \geq 0}\sum_{m \geq 0} \frac{z^{m - k}}{k!}. \] The coefficient of $z^{-1}$ comes from $k = m + 1$: \[ \operatorname{Res}_{z=0} f = \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(m + 1)!} = e - 1. \]
Integrals. Inside $|z| = \frac{1}{2}$ the only singularity is $0$, so $\oint_{|z| = 1/2} f\, \mathrm{d}z = 2\pi\iota(e - 1)$. Inside $|z| = 2$ there is also the simple pole $z = 1$, with $\operatorname{Res}_{z=1} f = \frac{e^{1}}{-1} = -e$. So \[ \oint_{|z| = 2} f\, \mathrm{d}z = 2\pi\iota(e - 1 - e) = -2\pi\iota. \] Check: for large $|z|$, $f(z) = -\frac{1}{z}\left( 1 + \frac{1}{z} + \cdots \right)\left( 1 + \frac{1}{z} + \cdots \right)$, whose $\frac{1}{z}$-coefficient is $-1$.

problems.title: Residues at essential singularities: $z^2\sin\frac{1}{z}$ and $e^{z + 1/z}$
problems.problem:
Find the residue at $z = 0$ of
  1. $z^2 \sin\dfrac{1}{z}$,
  2. $e^{z + 1/z}$.
problems.hint: • Use Laurent series; at an essential singularity there is no shortcut formula for the residue.
problems.solution:
(a) For $z \neq 0$, \[ z^2\sin\frac{1}{z} = z^2\left( \frac{1}{z} - \frac{1}{3!\,z^3} + \frac{1}{5!\,z^5} - \cdots \right) = z - \frac{1}{6z} + \frac{1}{120z^3} - \cdots. \] So $\operatorname{Res}_{z=0} = -\frac{1}{6}$, and $\oint_{|z|=1} z^2\sin\frac{1}{z}\, \mathrm{d}z = -\frac{\pi\iota}{3}$.
(b) $e^{z + 1/z} = e^{z}e^{1/z} = \sum_{m \geq 0}\frac{z^m}{m!}\sum_{k \geq 0}\frac{z^{-k}}{k!}$. The coefficient of $z^{-1}$ comes from $k = m + 1$: \[ \operatorname{Res}_{z=0} e^{z + 1/z} = \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{m!\,(m + 1)!} \approx 1.5906. \] (This is the value $I_1(2)$ of a modified Bessel function: the Laurent coefficients of $e^{\frac{t}{2}(z + 1/z)}$ are the Bessel functions $I_n(t)$.)

problems.title: $\oint \frac{e^z}{z^{n+1}}\, \mathrm{d}z$ and $\int_0^{2\pi} e^{\cos\theta}\cos(\sin\theta - n\theta)\, \mathrm{d}\theta = \frac{2\pi}{n!}$
problems.problem:
Let $n \geq 0$ be an integer.
  1. Show that $\displaystyle \oint_{|z| = 1} \frac{e^{z}}{z^{n+1}}\, \mathrm{d}z = \frac{2\pi\iota}{n!}$.
  2. Deduce that $\displaystyle \int_0^{2\pi} e^{\cos\theta}\cos(\sin\theta - n\theta)\, \mathrm{d}\theta = \frac{2\pi}{n!}$ and $\displaystyle \int_0^{2\pi} e^{\cos\theta}\sin(\sin\theta - n\theta)\, \mathrm{d}\theta = 0$.
problems.hint: • (a) is Cauchy's formula for the $n$th derivative, or the coefficient of $z^{-1}$ in $\sum \frac{z^{k - n - 1}}{k!}$. For (b), parametrise $z = e^{\iota\theta}$.
problems.solution:
(a) By Cauchy's integral formula for derivatives, $\oint_{|z|=1}\frac{e^z}{z^{n+1}}\, \mathrm{d}z = \frac{2\pi\iota}{n!}\left. \frac{\mathrm{d}^n}{\mathrm{d}z^n}e^z \right|_{z=0} = \frac{2\pi\iota}{n!}$. (Equivalently, the residue at $0$ is the coefficient $\frac{1}{n!}$ of $z^n$ in $e^z$.)
(b) With $z = e^{\iota\theta}$, $\mathrm{d}z = \iota e^{\iota\theta}\, \mathrm{d}\theta$ and $e^{z} = e^{\cos\theta}e^{\iota\sin\theta}$: \[ \oint_{|z|=1}\frac{e^z}{z^{n+1}}\, \mathrm{d}z = \iota\int_0^{2\pi} e^{\cos\theta}e^{\iota(\sin\theta - n\theta)}\, \mathrm{d}\theta. \] Equating with $\frac{2\pi\iota}{n!}$ and dividing by $\iota$: \[ \int_0^{2\pi} e^{\cos\theta}\left[ \cos(\sin\theta - n\theta) + \iota\sin(\sin\theta - n\theta) \right] \mathrm{d}\theta = \frac{2\pi}{n!}. \] Comparing real and imaginary parts gives both formulas. For $n = 0$: $\int_0^{2\pi} e^{\cos\theta}\cos(\sin\theta)\, \mathrm{d}\theta = 2\pi$, the mean value property for $e^z$ at $0$.

problems.title: Reflection: an entire function that is real on the real axis satisfies $f(\bar{z}) = \overline{f(z)}$
problems.problem: Let $f$ be entire and suppose $f(x) \in \mathbb{R}$ for every real $x$. Prove that $f(\bar{z}) = \overline{f(z)}$ for all $z \in \mathbb{C}$. Deduce that the nonreal zeros of $f$ occur in conjugate pairs.
problems.hint: • The Taylor coefficients $a_n = \frac{f^{(n)}(0)}{n!}$ can be computed using real increments only, so they are real.
problems.solution:
Since $f$ is entire, $f(z) = \sum_{n \geq 0} a_n z^n$ for all $z$, with $a_n = \frac{f^{(n)}(0)}{n!}$. The derivative of an analytic function can be computed as a limit along the real axis: $f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0,\ h \in \mathbb{R}} \frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$. If $f$ is real on $\mathbb{R}$, these real difference quotients are real, so $f'$ is real on $\mathbb{R}$; by induction every $f^{(n)}$ is real on $\mathbb{R}$. Hence all $a_n$ are real.
Therefore \[ f(\bar{z}) = \sum a_n \bar{z}^n = \sum \overline{a_n z^n} = \overline{\sum a_n z^n} = \overline{f(z)}. \]
Zeros. If $f(z_0) = 0$, then $f(\overline{z_0}) = \overline{f(z_0)} = 0$. So nonreal zeros come in conjugate pairs; for polynomials with real coefficients this is the familiar fact. (This is the simplest case of the Schwarz reflection principle.)

problems.title: Riemann's theorem on removable singularities
problems.problem: Let $f$ be analytic on the punctured disc $0 \lt |z - z_0| \lt r$ and bounded there. Prove that $z_0$ is a removable singularity: $f$ extends to an analytic function on $|z - z_0| \lt r$.
problems.hint: • Consider $h(z) = (z - z_0)^2 f(z)$, $h(z_0) = 0$. Show $h$ is complex differentiable at $z_0$ with $h'(z_0) = 0$.
problems.solution:
Let $|f| \leq M$ and define $h(z) = (z - z_0)^2 f(z)$ for $z \neq z_0$, $h(z_0) = 0$. Then $h$ is analytic on the punctured disc, and at $z_0$ \[ \left| \frac{h(z) - h(z_0)}{z - z_0} \right| = |z - z_0|\,|f(z)| \leq M|z - z_0| \to 0, \] so $h'(z_0) = 0$. Thus $h$ is analytic on the whole disc, with $h(z_0) = h'(z_0) = 0$.
Its Taylor series therefore starts at the quadratic term: $h(z) = \sum_{n \geq 2} c_n(z - z_0)^n$ on $|z - z_0| \lt r$. For $z \neq z_0$, \[ f(z) = \frac{h(z)}{(z - z_0)^2} = \sum_{n \geq 2} c_n (z - z_0)^{n - 2}, \] and this power series defines an analytic function on the whole disc. Setting $f(z_0) = c_2$ extends $f$ analytically.
The same proof works under the weaker hypothesis $\lim_{z \to z_0}(z - z_0)f(z) = 0$. Example: $\frac{\sin z}{z}$ is bounded near $0$, so $0$ is removable.

problems.title: The Casorati-Weierstrass theorem
problems.problem: Let $f$ have an essential singularity at $z_0$. Prove that for every $\delta > 0$, the image $f(\{ z : 0 \lt |z - z_0| \lt \delta \})$ is dense in $\mathbb{C}$.
problems.hint: • If some disc $|w - w_0| \lt \varepsilon$ is missed, consider $g(z) = \frac{1}{f(z) - w_0}$, which is bounded. Use Riemann's removable singularity theorem.
problems.solution:
Suppose not: there are $\delta > 0$, $w_0 \in \mathbb{C}$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $|f(z) - w_0| \geq \varepsilon$ for all $0 \lt |z - z_0| \lt \delta$. Then \[ g(z) = \frac{1}{f(z) - w_0} \] is analytic on the punctured disc and $|g| \leq \frac{1}{\varepsilon}$. By Riemann's theorem, $g$ extends analytically to $z_0$. Also $g \not\equiv 0$.
Now $f(z) = w_0 + \frac{1}{g(z)}$ near $z_0$.
  • If $g(z_0) \neq 0$, then $f$ extends analytically to $z_0$: the singularity is removable.
  • If $g$ has a zero of order $m \geq 1$ at $z_0$, then $\frac{1}{g}$, and hence $f$, has a pole of order $m$ at $z_0$.
Either way $z_0$ is not an essential singularity, a contradiction. Hence the image of every punctured neighbourhood is dense.
For $e^{1/z}$ at $0$, Picard's great theorem gives more: every value except $0$ is taken infinitely often.

problems.title: An entire function with a pole at $\infty$ is a polynomial
problems.problem: Let $f$ be entire, and suppose $g(w) = f(1/w)$ has a pole (of order $m$) at $w = 0$; that is, $f$ has a pole at $\infty$. Prove that $f$ is a polynomial of degree $m$.
problems.hint: • Write $f(z) = \sum_{n \geq 0} a_nz^n$. Then $g(w) = \sum a_nw^{-n}$ is the Laurent series of $g$ about $0$.
problems.solution:
Since $f$ is entire, $f(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n z^n$ for all $z$. Hence for $w \neq 0$, \[ g(w) = f\left( \frac{1}{w} \right) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n w^{-n}, \] and by uniqueness this is the Laurent series of $g$ on $0 \lt |w| \lt \infty$.
A pole of order $m$ at $w = 0$ means that the Laurent series has only finitely many negative powers, the lowest being $w^{-m}$ with nonzero coefficient. So $a_n = 0$ for $n > m$ and $a_m \neq 0$, i.e. \[ f(z) = a_0 + a_1z + \cdots + a_mz^m, \] a polynomial of degree $m$. Conversely a polynomial of degree $m \geq 1$ has a pole of order $m$ at $\infty$. (If $g$ had a removable singularity at $0$, $f$ would be bounded, hence constant by Liouville.)

problems.title: The only one-to-one entire functions are $az + b$
problems.problem: Prove that if $f$ is entire and one-to-one, then $f(z) = az + b$ with $a \neq 0$.
problems.hint: • Look at the singularity of $f(1/w)$ at $w = 0$. Removable: Liouville. Essential: Casorati-Weierstrass contradicts injectivity together with the open mapping theorem. So it is a pole: $f$ is a polynomial. A polynomial of degree $\geq 2$ is not injective.
problems.solution:
Consider $g(w) = f(1/w)$ near $w = 0$.
  • Removable: then $f$ is bounded for $|z| > 1$ and on $|z| \leq 1$, so constant by Liouville, not injective.
  • Essential: by Casorati-Weierstrass, $f(\{ |z| > 1 \})$ is dense in $\mathbb{C}$. But $U = f(\{ |z| \lt 1 \})$ is a nonempty open set (open mapping theorem), so it meets $f(\{ |z| > 1 \})$: some $f(z_1) = f(z_2)$ with $|z_1| \lt 1 \lt |z_2|$, contradicting injectivity.
So $g$ has a pole at $0$, and $f$ is a polynomial (previous problem), say of degree $n \geq 1$.
Degree $1$. Suppose $n \geq 2$. For each $c$, $f(z) = c$ has $n$ roots counted with multiplicity; injectivity forces a single root $z_c$ of multiplicity $n$, so $f'(z_c) = 0$. Different $c$ give different $z_c$, so $f'$ (a nonzero polynomial of degree $n - 1$) would have infinitely many zeros, which is impossible. Hence $n = 1$ and $f(z) = az + b$ with $a \neq 0$.
Consequently the conformal automorphisms of $\mathbb{C}$ are exactly the maps $z \mapsto az + b$, $a \neq 0$.

problems.title: The Gauss-Lucas theorem: the zeros of $p'$ lie in the convex hull of the zeros of $p$
problems.problem: Let $p$ be a nonconstant complex polynomial. Prove that every zero of $p'$ lies in the convex hull of the zeros of $p$.
problems.hint: • Write $p(z) = c\prod_k (z - z_k)$, so $\frac{p'(z)}{p(z)} = \sum_k \frac{1}{z - z_k}$. At a zero $w$ of $p'$ that is not a zero of $p$, take complex conjugates.
problems.solution:
Write $p(z) = c\prod_{k=1}^{n}(z - z_k)$ (zeros repeated according to multiplicity). Then for $p(z) \neq 0$, \[ \frac{p'(z)}{p(z)} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{z - z_k}. \]
Let $p'(w) = 0$. If $p(w) = 0$, then $w$ is one of the $z_k$ and certainly in the convex hull. Otherwise \[ 0 = \sum_{k} \frac{1}{w - z_k} = \sum_k \frac{\overline{w} - \overline{z_k}}{|w - z_k|^2}. \] Taking complex conjugates, $\sum_k \lambda_k (w - z_k) = 0$ with $\lambda_k = \frac{1}{|w - z_k|^2} > 0$. Hence \[ w = \frac{\sum_k \lambda_k z_k}{\sum_k \lambda_k}, \] a convex combination of the $z_k$ with positive weights. So $w$ lies in the convex hull of the zeros of $p$.
For real polynomials with only real zeros this recovers a consequence of Rolle's theorem: the zeros of $p'$ lie between the smallest and largest zeros of $p$.

problems.title: $\int_0^{2\pi} \ln\vert 1 - re^{\iota\theta} \vert\, \mathrm{d}\theta = 0$ for $0 \leq r \lt 1$
problems.problem:
Show that
    \[
        \int_0^{2\pi} \ln\left| 1 - re^{\iota\theta} \right| \mathrm{d}\theta = \begin{cases} 0, & 0 \leq r \lt 1, \\ 2\pi\ln r, & r > 1. \end{cases}
    \]
problems.hint: • For $r \lt 1$, $u(z) = \ln|1 - rz| = \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Log}(1 - rz)$ is harmonic on a disc containing $|z| \leq 1$; use the mean value property. For $r > 1$ factor out $re^{\iota\theta}$.
problems.solution:
$0 \leq r \lt 1$. For $|z| \lt \frac{1}{r}$, $\operatorname{Re}(1 - rz) > 0$, so $\operatorname{Log}(1 - rz)$ is analytic there and $u(z) = \ln|1 - rz| = \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Log}(1 - rz)$ is harmonic on a disc containing $|z| \leq 1$. By the mean value property, \[ \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} u(e^{\iota\theta})\, \mathrm{d}\theta = u(0) = \ln 1 = 0. \] (Alternatively, $\operatorname{Log}(1 - re^{\iota\theta}) = -\sum_{n \geq 1}\frac{r^ne^{\iota n\theta}}{n}$ converges uniformly, and each term integrates to $0$.)
$r > 1$. $|1 - re^{\iota\theta}| = r\left| 1 - r^{-1}e^{-\iota\theta} \right|$. Hence \[ \int_0^{2\pi} \ln|1 - re^{\iota\theta}|\, \mathrm{d}\theta = 2\pi\ln r + \int_0^{2\pi}\ln\left| 1 - r^{-1}e^{-\iota\theta} \right| \mathrm{d}\theta = 2\pi\ln r, \] the last integral being $0$ by the first case (substitute $\theta \mapsto -\theta$). (For $r = 1$ the integral is also $0$, as an improper integral.) This is a special case of Jensen's formula.

problems.title: The Fresnel integrals: $\int_0^\infty \cos x^2\, \mathrm{d}x = \int_0^\infty \sin x^2\, \mathrm{d}x = \sqrt{\pi/8}$
problems.problem:
Using the function $e^{\iota z^2}$ and the sector $0 \leq \arg z \leq \frac{\pi}{4}$, $|z| \leq R$, show that
    \[
        \int_0^{\infty} \cos(x^2)\, \mathrm{d}x = \int_0^{\infty} \sin(x^2)\, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}.
    \]
problems.hint: • On the ray $z = re^{\iota\pi/4}$, $\iota z^2 = -r^2$. On the arc, $|e^{\iota z^2}| = e^{-R^2\sin 2\varphi}$; use $\sin 2\varphi \geq \frac{4\varphi}{\pi}$ on $[0, \frac{\pi}{4}]$. Recall $\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}\, \mathrm{d}r = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}$.
problems.solution:
$f(z) = e^{\iota z^2}$ is entire, so its integral over the boundary of the sector is $0$ (Cauchy). The boundary consists of $[0, R]$, the arc $\Gamma_R: z = Re^{\iota\varphi}$, $0 \leq \varphi \leq \frac{\pi}{4}$, and the ray back from $Re^{\iota\pi/4}$ to $0$.
Ray. With $z = re^{\iota\pi/4}$: $z^2 = \iota r^2$, $e^{\iota z^2} = e^{-r^2}$, so this piece is $-e^{\iota\pi/4}\int_0^R e^{-r^2}\, \mathrm{d}r \to -e^{\iota\pi/4}\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}$.
Arc. $|e^{\iota z^2}| = e^{-R^2\sin 2\varphi} \leq e^{-4R^2\varphi/\pi}$, so \[ \left| \int_{\Gamma_R} f\, \mathrm{d}z \right| \leq \int_0^{\pi/4} e^{-4R^2\varphi/\pi} R\, \mathrm{d}\varphi \lt R \cdot \frac{\pi}{4R^2} = \frac{\pi}{4R} \to 0. \]
Conclusion. Letting $R \to \infty$: \[ \int_0^\infty e^{\iota x^2}\, \mathrm{d}x = e^{\iota\pi/4}\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2} = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2\sqrt{2}}(1 + \iota). \] Taking real and imaginary parts gives both integrals equal to $\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}} \approx 0.6267$. (The integrals converge as improper integrals: substituting $t = x^2$ gives $\int \frac{\cos t}{2\sqrt{t}}\, \mathrm{d}t$, convergent by Dirichlet's test.)

problems.title: An integral with a logarithm: $\int_0^\infty \frac{\ln x}{(1 + x^2)^2}\, \mathrm{d}x = -\frac{\pi}{4}$
problems.problem:
Use a suitable branch of $\log z$ and an indented semicircular contour to show that
    \[
        \int_0^{\infty} \frac{\ln x}{(1 + x^2)^2}\, \mathrm{d}x = -\frac{\pi}{4}.
    \]
problems.hint: • Take $f(z) = \frac{\log z}{(z^2 + 1)^2}$ with $-\frac{\pi}{2} \lt \arg z \lt \frac{3\pi}{2}$. On the negative real axis, $\log z = \ln|x| + \iota\pi$. The only pole in the upper half-plane is the double pole $z = \iota$.
problems.solution:
Let $f(z) = \frac{\log z}{(z^2 + 1)^2}$ with the branch $\log z = \ln|z| + \iota\arg z$, $-\frac{\pi}{2} \lt \arg z \lt \frac{3\pi}{2}$, analytic in the closed upper half-plane except at $0$. Integrate over $[\varepsilon, R]$, the semicircle $C_R$, $[-R, -\varepsilon]$, and the small semicircle $C_\varepsilon$ (clockwise).
Real axis. For $z = -x$ ($x > 0$), $\log z = \ln x + \iota\pi$. So the two segments together give \[ 2\int_\varepsilon^R \frac{\ln x}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\, \mathrm{d}x + \iota\pi\int_\varepsilon^R \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{(x^2 + 1)^2}. \] Semicircles. On $C_R$, $|f| \leq \frac{\ln R + \pi}{(R^2 - 1)^2}$, so the integral is at most $\pi R \cdot \frac{\ln R + \pi}{(R^2 - 1)^2} \to 0$; on $C_\varepsilon$ it is at most $\pi\varepsilon\frac{|\ln\varepsilon| + \pi}{(1 - \varepsilon^2)^2} \to 0$.
Residue at $\iota$ (double pole): \[ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}z}\left[ \frac{\log z}{(z + \iota)^2} \right]_{z = \iota} = \frac{1}{\iota(2\iota)^2} - \frac{2\log\iota}{(2\iota)^3} = \frac{\iota}{4} - \frac{2 \cdot \iota\pi/2}{-8\iota} = \frac{\iota}{4} + \frac{\pi}{8}. \] So the contour integral is $2\pi\iota\left( \frac{\iota}{4} + \frac{\pi}{8} \right) = -\frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\iota\pi^2}{4}$.
